title: Area-based conservation
definition: Area-based conservation with a nexus approach uses protected areas (Grorud-Colvert et al., 2021; IUCN, 2004; Meehan et al., 2020; Shafer, 2015), other effective conservation measures (OECMs) and other relevant area-based conservation strategies (Dudley et al., 2018; Grorud-Colvert et al., 2021) to conserve biodiversity across land and sea, including territories of IPLC. Based on a review of the literature, area-based conservation strategies were categorized into five types, but analysis focused on the first four on which spatially explicit data were available. Overall, area-based conservation has a positive impact on biodiversity by increasing or maintaining area in good condition, enhancing ecological function and diversity, and reducing land and sea degradation (e.g. Kawaka et al., 2017; Maini et al., 2023; Olsson et al., 2004; Soliku & Schraml, 2020). Biodiversity response option Global Regional National Subnational Local Long-term (11+ years) Medium-term (4-10 years) Short-term (1-3 years)

title: Halt conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity
definition: Halting the conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity for food production is a response option that can be applied globally (Jacobson et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2020; Riggio et al., 2020) and in the short-term, with long-term benefits. It has strong positive impacts across the nexus, although it has the potential for negative impacts on food production and access to food. Food demand is projected to drive agricultural expansion and the loss of 2-10 million km2 of ecosystems of high ecological integrity in coming decades (Alexandratos et al., 2012; Bajželj et al., 2014; Oakleaf et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2011; Willett, 2019; B. A. Williams et al., 2020; D. R. Williams et al., 2021). Halting this conversion could have a negative impact on food production and access to food, particularly in the Global South and for the most marginalized in society (Alexandratos et al., 2012; Bajželj et al., 2014; Oakleaf et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2011; Willett, 2019; B. A. Williams et al., 2020; D. R. Williams et al., 2021). However, this negative impact could be avoided by producing more food from existing agricultural and degraded land,), reducing demand by reducing food waste ) and shifting to sustainable healthy diets that require less land to support ) (Tilman et al., 2011; Willett, 2019; D. R. Williams et al., 2021). Halting conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity has very large positive impacts on biodiversity and climate change. Intact ecosystems are irreplaceable for conserving native species (Balmford, 2021; Watson et al., 2018); ecosystem function and resilience (Eigenbrod et al., 2015; Forzieri et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2018); reducing or preventing fragmentation (Brennan et al., 2022; Crooks et al., 2017; Haddad et al., 2015); and carbon storage and sequestration (Friedlingstein et al., 2022; Molotoks et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2019, 2021; D. R. Williams et al., 2018). Halting conversion of these ecosystems also benefits human health and well-being by reducing the probability of zoonotic disease transmission to people and livestock (Allen et al., 2017; Gottdenker et al., 2014; Rohr et al., 2019), reducing vulnerability to climate change and temperature extremes (Butt et al., 2023; IPCC, 2022) and benefiting mental, social and cultural well-being (IPBES, 2019a; Pascual et al., 2017). It also increases water provision by regulating streamflow, improving water quality and increasing precipitation, although there may be local-scale complexity in precipitation changes (Brauman et al., 2020; Hoek Van Dijke et al., 2022; Spracklen et al., 2018). Multiple actions exist for halting conversion. The most appropriate, effective and equitable actions will depend on social, economic, political and agricultural contexts. Halting conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity is at Technical Readiness Level 9; direct costs are relatively low, but local opportunity costs may be very high if the land is needed to meet food demand (Armstrong, 2023; Balmford & Whitten, 2003; J. M. H. Green et al., 2018; Waldron et al., 2013, 2017, 2022). This response option is aligned strongly with multiple international frameworks (CBD, 2023; UN, 2023; UNFCCC, 2015; United Nations, 2015). Alignment with national and local priorities, social acceptability and impacts on equity and IPLC will depend on the action taken, scale of opportunity costs, their distribution and their mitigation. There is limited evidence of transformative change potential for this response option alone, but it has high transformative potential when combined with yield-increasing response options. Approach

title: Forest conservation for health
definition: Forests are critical for human, animal and ecosystem health for their role in removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in exchange for oxygen. Their loss through removal and fire is a source of direct harm to human health, including through extensive air pollution and respiratory disease (E. W. Butt et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2015; Palmer, 2022; Spracklen & Garcia-Carreras, 2015; Wolff et al., 2021). However, deforestation continues to take place at alarming rates. Promoting forest conservation is a response option that can be applied globally wherever forests exist. Benefits and impacts are from local to global scales, with 60 million people, many IPLC, living within and wholly dependent on forests (McFarlane et al., 2019). Exposure to forests is also associated with positive health benefits in pregnancy and childhood (foetal growth, brain development, mental health in childhood, and prevention and reduction of childhood infectious diseases and malnutrition), adult life (mental and spiritual well-being and quality of life, and cardiometabolic health), and later stages of life (strong positive effects on cognitive decline and dementia, mental health and well-being, and longevity and mortality) (IUFRO, 2023). Forest conservation efforts enable these exposures and can also reduce malaria prevalence (Fornace et al., 2016; MacDonald & Mordecai, 2019). Water quality for both humans and ecosystems is improved by forest conservation, since an estimated 75 per cent of the world’s accessible freshwater comes from forested watersheds (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005). Forest conservation provides forest-based foods and products to an estimated one billion people (Maricé & Spalding, 2022). It is well established that the benefits of avoiding and reducing deforestation and promoting restoration can be significant for biodiversity (IPBES, 2019b). It also contributes to climate change mitigation, with nine countries having reported 8.82 Gt of greenhouse gas emission reductions due to reduced rates of deforestation and forest degradation under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change framework for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation and the role of conservation

title: Forest landscape restoration
definition: Forests and trees offer powerful tools for building inclusive, sustainable and resilient landscapes. They provide a multitude of benefits for people, including climate change mitigation and adaptation (IPCC, 2022), biodiversity habitat (Betts et al., 2017), water security (Calder et al., 2007; CIFOR, 2012; Ellison et al., 2017) and sources of food, energy, medicine and jobs (FAO, 2014, 2020). This forest-based bioeconomy plays a critical role in achieving climate neutrality (Grassi et al., 2021) and addressing nexus challenges (FAO, 2022; IUCN, 2021; Springgay et al., 2019). Forest landscape restoration goes beyond simply increasing tree cover (Ometto et al., 2023). It is a continuous process aiming to regain ecological functionality, improve human well-being and restore landscape functions in degraded areas (Chazdon, Gutierrez, et al., 2020; Guariguata, 2021; IUCN & WRI, 2014). This dynamic approach also aligns with existing nature-based solutions standards, contributing to the recovery of essential nature’s contributions to people (Sivadas, 2022). While many actors are committed to forest landscape restoration (Slobodian et al., 2020), successful large-scale implementation remains challenging due to complex ecological, social, policy, market and institutional factors (C. Hanson et al., 2015). Payment for forest ecosystem services has been proposed as a financing mechanism (Slobodian et al., 2020), with examples such as China's large-scale payment for forest ecosystem services policies (Xu et al., 2006). However, evidence for payment for forest ecosystem services schemes delivering both social and ecological benefits across large landscapes remains limited (Li et al., 2019; Ota et al., 2020). The Restoration Opportunities Assessment Methodology, successfully implemented in Rwanda (Cohen-Shacham et al., 2016; IUCN, 2016), offers a promising path forward by building on existing policies and targets. However, documenting the economic and social success of forest landscape restoration globally is crucial, as addressing social critiques of inappropriate afforestation (Adade Williams et al., 2020; Reyes-García & Benyei, 2019) is vital for long-term success. The complexity of forest landscape restoration as a socioecological nature-based solutions presents both challenges and opportunities (Stanturf et al., 2019). Spatial relationships within land-use systems can create trade-offs, such as increased crop raiding by wildlife due to forest proximity (Pfeifer et al., 2022) or unequal benefit distribution between local and external stakeholders (Platts et al., 2023). Such projects associated with agricultural land conversion can lead to social and ecological trade-offs for local communities due to direct losses in production, access restrictions, land tenure issues, justice and power asymmetries (Few, 2013; Few et al., 2017; Jindal et al., 2008; Lele, 2013; Sandbrook & Burgess, 2015). Extensive rangelands can synergize with recovered forests, enhancing biodiversity and pastoral livelihoods while addressing climate change and desertification concerns (Mansourian & Stephenson, 2023; Vetter, 2020). The risks and trade-offs depend on the activity’s nature, scale, agreed definitions, regulations and monitoring and adherence to key principles. Examples such as failed restoration projects in Northern Malawi highlight the importance of clear goals and community understanding (Höhl et al., 2020). Three key aspects for the success of forest landscape restoration are ecological and social balance, supportive policies, and monitoring and adaptation (IUCN, 2020c; Mansourian & Stephenson, 2023).

title: Restoration of coastal and marine systems
definition: Coastal and marine nature-based solutions, including coral, seagrass and mangrove restoration, aim to protect, conserve and restore ecosystems while enhancing human quality of life (Riisager-Simonsen et al., 2022). These actions aim to restore habitats essential for economies and livelihoods, and reduce vulnerabilities against natural disasters for communities relying primarily on nature’s contributions to people (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Giffin et al., 2021; Greiner et al., 2013; Westoby et al., 2020). Seagrass, mangrove, algae and shallow and deep coral reef restoration promote habitat integrity, connectivity and resilience, benefitting intraspecific genetic variation, biodiversity and ecosystem functioning and, thereby, food security and health (Acreman et al., 2020; Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Des Roches et al., 2021; Greiner et al., 2013; R. Hughes & Stachowicz, 2004; Montoya Maya et al., 2016; NOAA, 2023; Riisager-Simonsen et al., 2022; Sinclair et al., 2021; Westoby et al., 2020). Restoring seagrasses, seaweeds and mangroves also helps mitigate climate change through “blue carbon” sequestration (Eger et al., 2022; Greiner et al., 2013; Thorhaug et al., 2017). Restoration projects at the local scale are long-term processes that can take decades and require balancing of conservation goals, human needs and ecological values with other strategies to promote synergies at different scales (Westoby et al., 2020). Restoration efforts are facilitated by building and supporting trust and coordination in multi-stakeholder collaboration. This requires addressing concerns, breaking down social barriers, respecting traditional customs, implementing systematic planning and ensuring monitoring, financing and equal decision-making among scientists, traditional owners (e.g., IPLC), the private sector and governmental and non-governmental bodies (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Greiner et al., 2013; Z. Liu et al., 2016; Sinclair et al., 2021). This collaboration also brings additional benefits. For example, actively involving local communities and volunteers in restoration increases awareness of their ecosystem dependency. It also increases coordination between local stakeholders, with traditional knowledge, and national stakeholders in the implementation of restoration actions while reducing costs (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Greiner et al., 2013; Z. Liu et al., 2016; Sinclair et al., 2021). Such coordination exists, for example, in Australia, where coastal ecosystem management is a national environmental concern and coordination of stakeholder networks is implemented (Sinclair et al., 2021). New approaches for restoring marine and coastal ecosystems are needed, as this process requires long-term commitment due to the timescale of species growth and succession and impacts of global drivers such as climate change. Projects are often short-term and only measure success in terms of species survival, hindering the measurement of the full and long-term outcomes of restoration for ecosystem functioning and socioeconomic benefits for stakeholders, such as cost savings in managing for flood risk (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; M. Y. Hein et al., 2017; Z. Liu et al., 2016; Reguero et al., 2021; Sinclair et al., 2021; Westoby et al., 2020). Implementing metrics to evaluate cost-effectiveness, documenting the causes of failures and assessing impacts on society’s inclusion (e.g., cultural, educational, gender and health) across governance levels is a critical need (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Greiner et al., 2013; T. Liu et al., 2016; Westoby et al., 2020). Ethical considerations in ecological restoration also need to be addressed by governments and scientists. These include: the higher cost of restoration versus preserving ecosystems; matching actions to drivers of ecological degradation; careful selection of techniques and species used; identifying sites based on factors of ecological degradation; minimum ecological requirements for restoration; and evaluating small-scale actions before large-scale implementation (Bayraktarov et al., 2016; Z. Liu et al., 2016; Rogers et al., 2015; Sinclair et al., 2021; Westoby et al., 2020).

title: Restoration of inland water systems
definition: Inland water ecosystems, such as lakes, rivers, wetlands and other waterbodies are among the most degraded ecosystems globally. For example, more than 80 per cent of wetlands have been lost (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005), leading to a decline in their associated nature’s contributions to people (Reid et al., 2019; Schallenberg et al., 2013). Inland water systems have been heavily modified and face multiple threats, including water withdrawal for human use; impacts of other natural resource uses, such as extraction of aggregates in mining and impacts on biodiversity from fisheries (Cooke et al., 2023); and flow modification driven by flood management, dams and channelization (Dudgeon et al., 2006). Thus, their restoration is critical for both nature and people. The restoration of inland waters can encompass diverse activities that lead to healthier and more natural flows, cleaner states and the sustainable use of biodiversity (Palmer & Ruhi, 2019). Activities such as dam removal, reduced pollution and responsible fisheries restore the health of inland water ecosystems by maintaining key ecohydrological processes of natural flooding and fluvial connectivity (Arthington et al., 2023; Thieme et al., 2023). Inland water restoration requires a cohesive framework to guide the evaluation of freshwater nature’s contributions to people, their trade-offs and sustainable management that takes account of the multiple, sometimes conflicting, dimensions of human and biodiversity dependence (Dunham et al., 2018; Palmer & Ruhi, 2019; Vollmer et al., 2018). Besides contributing to the conservation of freshwater and terrestrial biodiversity, inland water restoration also interacts, largely positively, with the other nexus elements. It can support healthier wild-capture inland fisheries, which are crucial aquatic food systems for millions globally, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia (Craig et al., 2017). Access to an affordable source of protein and micronutrients is crucial for the health of vulnerable groups (O’Meara et al., 2021). Preserving riparian habitat, especially in upper catchment areas (Abell et al., 2019), positively contributes to water security by improving water quality and can be facilitated by urban-rural payment schemes like payment for ecosystem services (Bremer et al., 2016). Healthy inland waters are also significant contributors to global carbon capture (Mitsch et al., 2013; Wohl et al., 2017) and hence can contribute to climate change mitigation. However, some trade-offs exist, such as the impact of irrigation for food production on surface waterbodies and groundwater (D’Odorico et al., 2018) or reservoir construction for the water security of dense urban areas (He et al., 2021). The restoration of inland waters often poses a difficult governance challenge due to the presence of multiple diverse actors with sometimes conflicting objectives and power (Lynch et al., 2023). Some freshwater resource management strategies including Integrated Water Resources Management are viewed as top-down and may fail to recognize and account for the cultural and societal values of ecosystems (Gain et al., 2021; Ochoa-García & Rist, 2018; Schreier et al., 2014; N. Watson, 2014; Woodhouse & Muller, 2017). Community-based approaches are more inclusive (Karres et al., 2022) and customary ILK-based management systems of IPLC play a vital role for inland water conservation and restoration (Bielawski, 2021). While policies often account for inland waters as part of the terrestrial realm (Lynch et al., 2017), which can lead to underrepresentation or less relevant conservation and restoration efforts (Birnie-Gauvin et al., 2023; Reid et al., 2019), the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework mentions ‘inland waters’ specifically, including the importance of the contribution of ILK and IPLC customary systems to inland waters conservation and restoration.

title: Rewilding
definition: Rewilding is an open-ended restoration approach focused on the recovery of ecological processes and interactions. It is particularly relevant in the face of climate change, where uncertainties in ecosystem responses to interventions challenge prescriptions of specific end states in ecological restoration (Du Toit & Pettorelli, 2019). Rewilding initiatives are predominantly local or sub-national, but their integration into national policies and multilevel environmental governance remains limited (Fayet et al., 2022; Jepson et al., 2018). Evidence from large-scale passive rewilding, however, demonstrates the potential for significant long-term social and cultural transformation (Calaboni et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Molin et al., 2017; Navarro & Pereira, 2015; Ramankutty et al., 2010; Silva et al., 2017; Tedesco et al., 2023). Promising rewilding interventions include dam removal (Vahedifard et al., 2021), wetland and peatland restoration (Tanneberger et al., 2021), forest landscape restoration (Chazdon, Lindenmayer, et al., 2020; Stanturf & Mansourian, 2020) and closer-to-nature forestry (Dandy & Wynne-Jones, 2019). Contentious issues include the return of large carnivores (e.g., Davoli et al., 2022; Rode et al., 2021) and the substitution of costly agri-environmental measures with rewilding practices such as natural grazing (e.g., Schou et al., 2021). These controversies may be addressed with intermediate approaches such as agricultural rewilding, which combines ecological restoration with limited agricultural production (M. S. Corson et al., 2022), alongside with cultural change in views and values of nature. Rewilding can contribute to multiple nexus benefits (Carver et al., 2021; Perino et al., 2019; Root-Bernstein et al., 2017; Svenning, 2020). The well-documented biodiversity benefits of rewilding include habitat creation, restoration of ecological processes and improved connectivity (Eckerter et al., 2022; Garrido et al., 2019; Hart et al., 2023; Paillet et al., 2010), particularly in expanding the range and abundance of keystone wildlife species (Chapron et al., 2014; P. J. Seddon et al., 2014). However, mitigation of biological invasions needs more evidence (Derham et al., 2018; Mungi et al., 2023). The removal of dams and dikes, by enabling the up-and down-stream movement of aquatic wildlife and sediments and reconnecting rivers to their floodplains, benefits freshwater and marine biodiversity and water quantity and quality (Bednarek, 2001; Habel et al., 2020; Stanley & Doyle, 2003). These biodiversity benefits can support food security and health through provisioning of wild foods (Ingram et al., 2021) and other non-timber forest products (Wiersum, 2017). Climate change benefits of rewilding are less documented and likely context-dependent (Fayet & Verburg, 2023). The rewetting of wetlands and peatlands, forest secondary succession, proforestation (the protection of existing forests, including degraded and secondary forests, towards full ecological maturity) and changes in trophic networks that increase soil carbon pools (Kreyling et al., 2021; Moomaw et al., 2019; Schwieger et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023) are promising for climate change mitigation. Benefits for climate change adaptation through enhanced ecosystem and social resilience are also expected. Rewilding can be implemented in diverse ways following guideline principles (Carver et al., 2021), but its social and economic impacts remain understudied. The involvement of local communities, particularly IPLC, and considerations of equity are central challenges (A. Martin et al., 2021; Mustonen et al., 2022). The environmental and economic costs and benefits of scaling out rewilding initiatives, and the development of novel policies and markets to enable it (Bateman & Balmford, 2023; Schulte to Bühne et al., 2022), present challenges for widespread adoption and may require cultural shifts (Mikołajczak et al., 2021; Van Meerbeek et al., 2019; Wynne-Jones, 2022).

title: Restore soil health
definition: Soils are the basis for producing more than 95 per cent of the food society eats (FAO, 2017; Kraamwinkel et al., 2021). Soil erosion by water is estimated to annually reduce global agricultural food production by 33.7 million tonnes (Sartori et al., 2019). Reverting soil degradation is central to restoring the productive capacity of degraded lands (R. Lal, 2004; UNCCD, 2022). Healthy soils constitute the foundation of agriculture and a critical resource providing society with food, feed, fibre and clean water (Kibblewhite et al., 2008). Restoration of degraded soils and conservation of soil productivity in agriculture is associated with management practices that increase soil organic carbon content (FAO & ITPS, 2021; Paustian et al., 2016). Soil organic carbon influences key soil functions such as crop yield and biomass production; storage and regulation of soil carbon, nutrient and water; control of erosion; filtering of wastes and pollutants from water that may compromise access to healthy food and well-being; and providing habitat for soil biodiversity (Adhikari & Hartemink, 2016; R. Lal, 2016). International efforts led by the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity, particularly its Plan of Action (2020-2030) for the International Initiative for the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Soil Biodiversity led by the Global Soil Partnership hosted at FAO, have triggered increased interest in soil restoration, particularly the restoration of soil functions driven by soil organic carbon and biodiversity (Cowie et al., 2018; Minasny et al., 2017; Van Der Putten et al., 2023). Recent evidence highlights the significant impact that the presence of earthworms alone can have on global food production, with contributions estimated at 6.5 per cent of global cereal production and 2.3 per cent of legume production, corresponding to over 140 million metric tons annually (Fonte et al., 2023). Management practices that enhance perennial vegetation significantly contribute to enhancing soil organic carbon content (Bayala et al., 2020; Bossio et al., 2020; P. Smith et al., 2020). Agroforestry has been increasingly recognized and practiced as a multifunctional land management option that can simultaneously contribute to income, food security and nutrition, soil health and carbon restoration, the conservation of biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people, and climate change adaptation and mitigation (Barrios et al., 2018, 2023; Mbow et al., 2014; Muchane et al, 2020; Nabuurs et al., 2022; Rosenstock et al., 2019; Terasaki Hart et al., 2023). Perennial ground cover through hedges, food-bearing shrubs and grass stripes are important means to broaden agroforestry options in agricultural landscapes. Food producing perennial options can be means to mediate the challenges posed by integration of trees in some environments where competition is high to produce sufficient food from limited land and water resources (Nyaga et al., 2015; Sida et al., 2018). Shrubs, vines and other semi-perennial crop integration can also address gender equity barriers as access to input and output markets and the right to grow trees is often limited for women farmers and women-headed households. Agroforestry has high established benefits across the nexus of biodiversity, food, health, climate change, energy, land and natural resource management (Ickowitz et al., 2022; van Noordwijk et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the success at scale of perennial revegetation efforts to recover soil health needs to be socially acceptable, economically feasible and in alignment with political priorities (UNCCD, 2020). This is well illustrated by the Great Green Wall Initiative in Africa which has evolved to embrace the need to include multiple stakeholder concerns and respect traditional customs, implement systematic planning and monitoring, and secure financing and ensure equity in decision-making among stakeholders.

title: Mangrove conservation and restoration for health
definition: Disaster risks from coastal hazards that threaten lives and livelihoods such as flooding, storms, tsunamis and sea level rise can be mitigated by nature-based solutions provided by mangroves. Mangrove conservation and restoration can be applied globally within the natural range of mangroves which are also key ecological niches at the interface between land and water in the tropics and subtropics. The ongoing destruction of mangrove is a threat to human, animal and ecosystem health. Mangrove conservation and restoration has synergies across health and other elements of the nexus. Its health benefit is based on the combination of significant reduction of lives lost from extreme events (Das & Vincent, 2009) and the provision of medicinal plants and animals (UNEP, 2006), although associated with mosquitoes (Awuku-Sowah et al., 2022; Ewel et al., 1998). More than 1 billion people live within 50 km of mangrove forests potentially benefit from them (UNEP, 2006). This response option improves water quality by filtration and absorption of effluents from aquaculture operations (Sulochanan et al., 2022; UNEP, 2006) and land-based sources of pollution (Mohamed et al., 2009). Mangroves provide shrimp and fish for healthy and culturally appropriate food (Ewel et al., 1998) and are an important support for fisheries due to their function as fish nurseries (UNEP, 2006). Maintaining and restoring mangroves helps to promote biodiversity by increasing the area of mangroves in good condition and providing critical habitat for an estimated 341 threatened species of reptiles, amphibians, mammals, fishes and birds (Carugati et al., 2018; Maricé & Spalding, 2022). Restoring and conserving mangroves aligns with multiple international frameworks and is explicitly included in and actioned through the national priorities of many countries. Recognition of broad health benefits of mangroves is uneven but disaster risk reduction, including for climate resilient health systems, is one driver of action (WHO, 2022b). In the absence of health coverage, mangroves are protected locally as an important source of traditional medicines (Awuku-Sowah et al., 2023). Summing up all measured goods and services, the total economic value of managing intact mangroves is substantially higher than conversion to aquaculture (UNEP, 2006). The response option is technically feasible, provides fair distribution of costs and benefits to communities involved, and allows for participation of local stakeholders in decision-making and implementation. It is equitable in that it can protect the local use of mangroves by local, vulnerable groups from competition with outsiders (Glaser & Da Silva Oliveira, 2004). It also facilitates a shift in views and values of mangrove forest from short-term extraction to long-term stewardship and sustainable use.

title: Wetland conservation and restoration
definition: A huge quantity of carbon is stored in peatlands and wetlands (e.g., 500–850 Pg C, Turetsky et al., 2015), but around 12 per cent of global peatlands have been drained and degraded (UNEP, 2022). Restoration and reduced conversion of peatlands and non-coastal wetlands involves rewetting by blocking drainage channels and can include other interventions such as erosion prevention by stabilizing eroded peats through physical means (mounding or adding netting) and revegetation (IUCN, 2016). Restoration can be applied anywhere that peatlands / wetlands have been degraded. Peatlands occur on all continents and cover 3-4 per cent on the Earth’s land surface (UNEP, 2022). The global mitigation potential for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and increasing carbon storage through peatland / wetland restoration is 0.6-2.0 GtCO2e/ yr, but there are no global estimates of adaptation potential (P. Smith, Calvin, et al., 2020; P. Smith et al., 2022). Degraded peatlands store less water than intact peatlands. Peatland restoration upstream in catchments is used as a nature-based solution for flood control, e.g., managing flood / highwater peaks downstream after heavy rainfall. The storage and regulation of water flow in wetlands may also buffer against the effects of drought (Munang, Thiaw, Alverson, Liu, et al., 2013; Munang, Thiaw, Alverson, Mumba, et al., 2013). While tropical peats in South-East Asia have been substantially drained and cleared for non-food commodities (e.g., pulp and paper, and oil palm), large areas of tropical peatlands have been cleared for food production, and their restoration could displace food production and damage local food supply in these areas. The same is true for cultivated northern peatlands (Miettinen et al., 2016). At a local level, while peatland restoration on land used for agriculture could displace food production, the impacts to regional and global food security would be minimal (Humpenöder et al., 2018). For health, rewetting of formerly drained areas in regions where vector-borne diseases (from organisms which have part of their lifecycle in water) are endemic, could lead to a greater disease burden, but can improve public health through decreased fire-caused pollutants locally and distributed more widely (Dale & Connelly, 2012; Griscom et al., 2017). Large-scale changes in the water balance of peatlands and type of vegetation influence evaporation, which has a cooling effect on the local or regional climate. This can influence local or regional weather cycles. Rewetting drained peatlands can reduce heat, and reduced heat has a positive impact on public health (Sadeghi et al., 2022). Peatlands in good condition support a range of specialist and unique species, so peatland/wetland restoration will benefit biodiversity (UNEP, 2022). Globally, only a small percentage of peatlands are protected and, in many regions, there is no protection at all (UNEP, 2022). Hence, protection of peatlands / wetlands will improve the area of land protected, which enhances habitat connectivity and reduces fragmentation of intact peatlands, making them more resilient to, for example, the threat of erosion (IUCN, 2016). Drained and degraded peatlands lose many peatland functions, including carbon and water storage, so peatland / wetland restoration also restores these INCLUDING RELEVANT ASPECTS OF THE ENERGY SYSTEM ecological functions and a range of NCP (P. Smith et al., 2019). Restoration and reduced conversion of peatlands/ wetlands is at TRL 8-9 (Babiker et al., 2022), but there could be public acceptance issues around restoring wetlands in areas where vector-borne diseases are endemic due to health concerns (Dale & Connelly, 2012). It aligns strongly with policies to improve soil and water quality, to combat land degradation and desertification and to tackle climate change (P. Smith, Calvin, et al., 2020). Costs can be relatively high. Humpenöder et al. (2020) use one-time costs of $7,000 ha-1 (2005 market exchange rate) for the initial rewetting, and recurring costs of $200 ha-1 yr-1 for maintenance, based on an indicative cost estimate of £200–10,000 ha-1 for rewetting, and £25–400 ha-1 yr-1 for maintenance (Glenk & Martin-Ortega, 2018; Moxey & Moran, 2014). Monitoring, reporting and verification costs, and opportunity costs associated with lost agricultural production, may be high. Direct economic benefits are limited, though carbon finance has provided income for peatland / wetland protection / restoration projects (Joosten, 2012). In terms of equity, it provides benefits to IPLC (e.g. Suwarno et al., 2016), and can enable inclusive and participatory processes (e.g. Tan et al., 2023).

title: Restoration of coastal and marine ecosystems for carbon sequestration
definition: Coastal blue carbon ecosystems (CBCE) are marine habitats composed of rooted vegetation (Nellemann et al., 2009), namely mangroves (Giri et al., 2011; Spalding et al., 2010), seagrasses (Duarte, 1991; Green & Short, 2003) and salt marshes (Mason et al., 2023). Some authors also include marine sediments, components of the biological carbon cycle (e.g., whales), calcifying organisms and macroalgae in blue carbon estimates. This response option focuses on mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes, which are responsible for 45 per cent of the organic carbon burial in the ocean (Duarte et al., 2005, 2013), and the emerging macroalgae. CBCE have many impacts on climate change mitigation and adaptation, as well as the nexus elements of biodiversity, water, food and health. Mangrove forests support Indigenous institutions and cosmologies around the world, e.g., African Joola (Diatta et al., 2020), American Wayampi (Dugast, 2002), in Brunei (Islam & Yahya, 2017) or Indian festivals and celebrations (Jalais, 2014; Uddin et al., 2013). As such, mangroves sustain ILK (Walters et al., 2008) often by women (Chuku et al., 2022; Crow & Carney, 2013). Kelp forests are central to Canadian Haida Gwaii people, whose ethics and values have been adapted to support restoration and are aligned with ecosystem-based management principles (Eger et al., 2022). Kelp forests are also part of the traditional knowledge of the Kawésqar people of southern Chile (Friedlander et al., 2021). Saltmarshes are sacred places for the North American Gullah Geechee (Seabrook, 2012) and native Cajuns (Gramling & Hagelman, 2005). In contrast, seagrass meadows have limited societal recognition (Unsworth et al., 2019), although examples of local communities’ involvement exist in the Philippines (Quevedo et al., 2020), the Solomon Islands (Lauer & Aswani, 2010) or Zanzibar (de la Torre-Castro & Rönnbäck, 2004). They also play a role in preserving valuable

title: Agroecology*
definition: Agroecology is an integrated approach that simultaneously applies ecological and social concepts and principles to the design and management of food and agricultural systems (FAO, 2018; HLPE, 2019). Agroecology is supported by

title: Sustainable inland fisheries
definition: Increasing knowledge to improve inland fisheries assessments and management is a response option that can be applied globally on all managed inland waters (Funge-Smith, 2018). It also furthers equity initiatives and aligns with international framework targets through increased catch that can reduce poverty, while also increase economic stability and improved status in the community (Lynch et al., 2020). However, results of the knowledge generated from this option, how that knowledge can be used and how practitioners choose to implement it will affect its impact (FAO, 2021). Therefore, there is a high-level of context-dependence inherent in this response option. Well-managed fisheries are dependent on suitable water quality, as this directly affects fish populations and communities and fisheries' health. However, there is high uncertainty on the valuation of ecosystem services such as water quality (Keeler et al., 2012). Therefore, the lack of appropriate data and the lack of understanding of the effects of water quality changes on fish and fisheries remains unresolved (Bunnell et al., 2021). Evidence on how the physiology of a fish responds to changes in temperature, water quality and other stressors would help gain a better understanding on how to manage these fisheries in the future (Y. Chen et al., 2016; Whitney et al., 2016). Therefore, increased knowledge around fisheries management is likely to benefit water for both humans and ecosystems (Funge-Smith, 2018). Inland fisheries have an important role in sustainably feeding growing human populations, as they deliver quality nutrition to some of the world’s most vulnerable populations in a manner that is both accessible and affordable (Funge-Smith, 2018). They help meet SDGs 2, 6 and 15 and can play a role in cost-efficient water quality management (Jůza et al., 2019). Inland fisheries catch represents ~12 per cent of global fishery production, however, values may be considerably higher given data and reporting limitations. Thus, further assessments would improve understanding of inland fisheries as a source of food to support nutritional security and overall well-being (FAO, 2021). For other aspects of health, there is a need for additional information on well-being. Implementing fisheries management plans can positively impact freshwater biodiversity, which can serve as an indicator of ecosystem health (Funge-Smith, 2018). In general, the level of knowledge on freshwater biodiversity (i.e., species richness, endemism, production, level of endangerment and value) is poor or out of date (FAO, 2021; Funge-Smith, 2018; Taylor & Bartley, 2016). Increased knowledge would allow countries to assess the status of their ecosystems to predict future impacts and quantify the effects of management on fisheries for their future needs in food security, livelihoods, recreation and investment (FAO, 2021). There is limited evidence on the transformative change potential for this response option alone, though when combined with others, it may have high transformative potential and may be considered a cross-cutting option for addressing interactions across the nexus.

title: Manage alien species
definition: The management of aquatic invasive alien species (invasive alien species) to conserve freshwater biodiversity requires an understanding of the ecology of invasive alien species populations and their interactions within and across trophic levels of fishes (Conrad et al., 2016). Invasive alien species cover a wide range of taxonomic groups (macrophytes, phytoplankton, zooplankton, benthic invertebrates and fish) across different trophic guilds (primary producers, filter collectors, omnivores and predators) and habitats (rivers, lakes, and estuaries), with strong and pervasive negative impacts on native communities and aquatic habitat functioning (Gallardo et al., 2016). Economic wealth affects the risk of invasive alien species because increases in economic growth may encourage sectors to benefit from alien species (IPBES, 2023b). For example, invasive Blue Catfish in the Chesapeake Bay in the eastern United States of America create recreational fisheries and economic benefits but also are detrimental to native fish populations (Paukert et al., 2021). The main invasion vectors differ between high-income countries (imports of pets and plants) and low-income countries (shipping of goods and people), with the latter tending to have more reactive national policies. Countries with high incidence risk for invasive alien species tend to have proactive capacities, yet there are only a few examples of strong policies even in those countries with high incidence (Early et al., 2016). Furthermore, species interactions with native species might hinder the ‘ideal’ timing and success for this response option (IPBES, 2023b; Lampert et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2009). The literature review focused on reducing pathways for aquatic invasive alien species as these are one of the top five priorities for conserving freshwater biodiversity (Dudgeon et al., 2006; Gallardo et al., 2016) and addressing biodiversity loss (IPBES, 2019). The geographic scope of aquatic invasive alien species is well established as global (Cuthbert et al., 2021; Early et al., 2016; Gallardo et al., 2016; Pyšek et al., 2020), but with interventions at local levels along the invasion pathways from source to establishment and persistence (Kühn & Klotz, 2007). These interventions are well established with mostly positive outcomes that can help ‘bend the curve’ on freshwater biodiversity loss (Tickner et al., 2020). The temporal scale is variable and depends on the specific aquatic invasive alien species (e.g., Masson et al., 2016). Most studies suggest that invasive alien species have variable impacts on water, such as changing turbidity, which affects water quality, or increasing water filtration and purity (Pejchar & Mooney, 2009). Managing aquatic invasive alien species could result in better water saving outcomes, but this has not been quantified. Managing invasive alien species often focuses on removals to control the species/taxa but can also include prevention, but both measures have mixed success (IPBES, 2023a). Prevention of invasive species is more cost effective than actual removals or control once a species is present (IPBES, 2023b). However, prevention is complex as some aquatic invasive alien species contribute to food security by providing foods to local communities and economic benefit (Lee & Gordon, 2006; Paukert et al., 2021). Some invasive alien species also outcompete native species which could also provide food security (Britton, 2023). Aquatic invasive alien species can have co-benefits for climate change adaptation and may be carbon sinks or sources (Pejchar & Mooney, 2009). However, knowledge is still inconclusive because of the variety of aquatic invasive alien species that need to be assessed and the range of conditions where they occur. There are also health benefits, such as invasive alien species contribution to disease regulation and recreational activities (Cambray, 2003), but also health disbenefits, such as invasive alien species acting as new vectors of disease (Pejchar & Mooney, 2009). Management of aquatic invasive alien species is contested. Although they provide services and livelihoods (e.g., food, materials, tourism, etc.) that have economic benefits (Larson et al., 2011), those benefits typically do not mitigate their negative impacts, given that the total cost of alien species effects on humans is estimated to be over $423 billion (IPBES, 2023a). Acceptance of invasive alien species management is variable and depends on the local cost and benefits, which are often unresolved (Hanley & Roberts, 2019). In addition, many smallholders, fishers and communities already manage aquatic invasive alien species (Reo & Ogden, 2018) using traditional knowledge and experience (Magellan, 2019). Overall, the management of aquatic invasive alien species is well established in many political priorities and can be technically feasible, but feasibility depends on context (IPBES, 2023a). In connected systems such as rivers, eradication can be ineffective (IPBES, 2023a). However, managing aquatic alien species aligns with global goals for climate smart food production, biodiversity and food and water security (Hussner et al., 2017). The implementation of management interventions for aquatic invasive alien species is linked to many global frameworks (e.g., target 7 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework; UN Food System Pathways 2

title: Ecological intensification – croplands
definition: Ecological Intensification “entails the environmentally friendly replacement of anthropogenic inputs and/or enhancement of crop productivity, by including regulating and supporting ecosystem services management in agricultural practices” (Bommarco et al., 2013) (e.g., pollination, pest regulation, soil formation) and is the basis of agroecological practices. Ecological intensification practices span traditional and modern innovations originating from local, Indigenous, farmer and scientific knowledge systems (Caron et al., 2014; Geertsema et al., 2016; Raj et al., 2021). Garibaldi et al. (2019) proposed ten science-based policy recommendations for ecological intensification of agriculture with recent work suggesting that minimum habitat per km2 should be between 10-25 per cent (Mohamed et al., 2022): 1) Enhance above-and belowground species diversity 2) Reduce synthetic inputs 3) Enhance soil health 4) Maintain and/or restore natural and semi-natural habitat areas with recent values suggested to at least 10-25 per cent per km2 (Mohamed et al., 2022) 5) Enhance habitat diversity 6) Implement a landscape design plan to integrate practices 7) Protect and efficiently use water resources 8) Evaluate agricultural productivity and ecosystem services over the long-term 9) Consider multiple outcome benefits

title: Ecological intensification – rangelands
definition: Rangelands cover a greater area than any other terrestrial food system. Ecological intensification of rangelands can make them more productive while also providing benefits to other nexus elements. This can be achieved through a variety of mechanisms, including regenerative grazing (modifying the intensity and duration of grazing to mimic natural systems), pyric herbivory (integration of fire and grazing in a shifting mosaic of patches), silvopasture and fence-free herding.

title: Ecological intensification – aquatic foods
definition: Ecological Intensification of aquatic foods focuses on enhancing the ecological processes within aquatic ecosystems, such as nutrient cycling, habitat structure maintenance, and trophic interactions, to increase the productivity and resilience of freshwater and marine food sources. Ecological intensification of aquatic food systems is a response option that can be applied across much of the world’s marine and freshwater systems, with consistently positive impacts on other nexus elements. Benefits are greatest when combined with halting the conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity, both aquatic and terrestrial, and reducing demand through reduced food loss and waste and shifting to sustainable healthy diets

title: Increase soil organic carbon
definition: Soil organic carbon (SOC) content can be increased through management interventions in croplands, grazing lands and managed forests that either increase carbon inputs to the soil, cause the carbon to persist longer in the soil, or reduce losses from the soil by decreasing soil disturbance or placing carbon at deeper layers of the soil (P. Smith, 2016). Carbon inputs can occur through traditional forms such as litter and manure, but also through newer technologies such as biochar (P. Smith, 2016). Increasing SOC content is a response option that can be applied globally on all managed land (FAO & ITPS, 2015). It is beneficial across all nexus elements, with very large potentials for climate change mitigation potential (0.4–8.6 Gt CO2eq/yr) and adaptation (up to 3200 million people potentially benefiting) (P. Smith, Calvin, et al., 2020). However, soil carbon sinks, like all biological carbon sinks, are time-limited (due to sink saturation) and reversible (through, for example, poor management or extreme events such as fire) and could be impacted by climate change (C. Jones et al., 2005). For water, well-managed soils with high SOC content have high infiltration capacity that increases green water (available for plants to enhance crop production and nature) and regulates blue water (fewer floods). Soils also function as a filter for pollutants, improving water quality (Cheng et al., 2021; Keesstra et al., 2021). For food and health, higher SOC levels also give rise to higher crop yields (Qiao et al., 2022) which could alleviate the burden of undernutrition in some areas (with a subsequent strong positive impact on health), though there is limited evidence on its impact on food access or the nutritional value of food. For biodiversity, soil organic matter is a headline indicator of soil health. With around 120 thousand km2 of land lost to degradation every year (IPBES, 2018), management practices that increase SOC would help increase the area in better condition, thereby improving soil health and biodiversity. Since increasing SOC content is practiced only on managed land, it has no impact on the area of land protected or other aspects of native biodiversity, but practices that lead to increased soil organic matter also tend to improve soil biodiversity (P. Smith et al., 2015). Increased SOC also improves ecological functioning, since soils higher in SOC function better than degraded soils with lower levels (De Deyn & Kooistra, 2021). Additionally, it also improves ecological resilience as soils higher in SOC are more resilient to drought and floods and less prone to soil erosion (Lal, 2015). Practices to increase SOC levels, which increase carbon inputs or decrease carbon losses, are already widely implemented through best management practices in agriculture (e.g., conservation agriculture) and forestry (TRL 9: Babiker et al., 2022). There are no known social acceptability issues with implementing this response option and it aligns strongly with policies to improve soil and water quality, to combat land degradation and desertification, to increase food production and to tackle climate change (P. Smith, Calvin, et al., 2020). Increasing SOC is a relatively low-cost option (P. Smith, 2016) though monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) costs can be high (P. Smith, Soussana, et al., 2020). Since it leads to higher yields and improves resilience to drought and erosion (Lal, 2015), it enhances economic benefits and reduces risk. In terms of equity, many IPLC management practices are known to result in high carbon levels and biodiverse soils (McElwee, 2021). For example, traditional homestead and landscape-level interventions in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands of India focusing on biodiversity, including the use of over 7500 plant species, contributed to SOC improvement through the enhancement of ecosystem diversity and resilience (Ichikawa, 2018).

title: Integrated multitrophic aquaculture
definition: Integrated multitrophic aquaculture is a traditional aquaculture method that has been practiced in Asia and the Mediterranean since ancient times (Chopin, 2013). The method involves using the waste products and uneaten food generated by a high tropic level species (e.g., farmed fish) to cultivate other species at lower trophic levels, thereby reducing waste and mitigating its negative impacts on the environment and promoting sustainable food production (Chopin et al., 2012; Cottier-Cook, et al., 2016). The system is based on the idea of combining several species, including fish and shrimp as main target species, with bivalves that feed on suspended particulate organic matter, seaweeds that convert dissolved inorganic carbon and nutrients into biomass, and occasionally deposit feeders on the bottom sediment such as echinoderms (Altamirano et al., 2022; Chopin et al., 2012; Eyrolles et al., 2018; FAO, 2022a). Recently, there has been a shift towards combing sustainable food production with climate change adaptation and mitigation measures (UNEP, 2023). This includes focusing on seaweed cultivation to increase CO2 sequestration, as well as mitigating the negative effects of climate change such as acidification on shellfish aquaculture (Hamilton et al., 2022). As a derivative, there is also a movement to integrate CO2 sequestration by natural blue carbon ecosystems with aquaculture (Hori et al., 2021). Recently seaweed farming has become a major crop of integrated multitrophic aquaculture in some regions (UNEP, 2023), while finfish and shellfish aquaculture, previously the major product, is sometimes being used to alleviate nutrient limitation on seaweed growth (J. K. Kim et al., 2017). Integrated multitrophic aquaculture exhibits comparatively lower environmental impact and smaller spatial footprints compared with both capture fisheries and land-based agriculture (Gentry et al., 2020; Stentiford et al., 2020). This is further emphasized in the shift from fed fish to non-fed species, such as filter feeding bivalves, algal grazers, detritivores and autotrophic plants (mainly macroalgae), as these are considered some of the lowest impact aquaculture in ambient waters, resulting in the lowest negative impact on the environment and biodiversity (Stentiford et al., 2020). In terms of food and biodiversity, integrated multitrophic aquaculture can provide nutritious and safe food to consume with lower risk of exposure to harmful microbial and chemical contaminants (Stentiford et al., 2020). In the case of seaweeds and bivalve farming, culture platforms can simultaneously act as nurseries for native biodiversity and boost productivity of wild organisms (FAO, 2022a; Gentry et al., 2020). Integrated multitrophic aquaculture effectively combines multiple species to utilize waste products for cultivation, enhancing environmental sustainability and providing nutritious, low-impact food while fostering biodiversity and aiding in climate change adaptation. By enhancing resource efficiency and profitability through reduced feed costs and improved overall yield, supports local communities by offering diverse employment opportunities and improving food security. Additionally, the adoption of integrated multitrophic aquaculture aligns with global sustainability goals and fosters international cooperation in sustainable aquaculture practices.

title: Forest-based practices to address climate change
definition: Optimized management of existing forests, prevention of forest losses, reforestation, forest restoration and afforestation are among the main multi-purpose and cost-effective options for climate change mitigation via solutions based on nature (Kaarakka et al., 2021). Although forest carbon sequestration and storage are not a substitute for urgent reductions of fossil CO2 emissions (Anderson et al., 2019; Seddon et al., 2021), the conservation, restoration and sustainable management of forests offer contributions to achieve climate and biodiversity targets. For example, reduced deforestation and forest degradation plays an important role in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Likewise, improved and sustainable forest management (ISFM) maintains and enhances the social, economic, ecological and cultural values of forests for the benefit of present and future generations (Kaarakka et al., 2021; MacDicken et al., 2015). Reduced forest degradation, forest restoration and ISFM are strongly interconnected in terms of their objectives and approach. The mitigation potential of reduced deforestation and forest degradation is high (up to 5.8 Gt CO2-eq/yr) (P. Smith, Calvin, et al., 2020). ISFM also has a high mitigation potential as it maintains forest carbon sinks (estimates are up to about 2 GtCO2/yr) (Griscom et al., 2017; Roe et al., 2019), it makes forests more resilient to climate-driven disturbances and it temporarily stores carbon in long-lived products (Anderegg et al., 2020; Daigneault & Favero, 2021). Reforestation has a large mitigation potential (Roe et al., 2019). It can be implemented globally, but the highest benefits occur in the tropics where carbon sequestration rates and concentration of endangered species that live in the forests are high (Locatelli et al., 2015; Prudhomme et al., 2020). In the tropics, biophysical effects of reforestation also reinforce the cooling contributions from CO2 removal, while in areas with seasonal snow cover, the cooling benefits of reforestation are reduced due to changes in surface albedo (Perugini et al., 2017; Windisch et al., 2021). In terms of forest restoration potential, global forest carbon storage is currently below its natural potential (with an estimated total deficit of 226 GtC). Since most of this potential lies in areas with existing forests where human footprint is low, effective ecosystem protection and management can promote forest restoration up to 139 GtC by allowing forests to recover to maturity (Mo et al., 2023). All forest-based solutions for climate action have the potential to co-deliver across multiple nexus elements. Interactions are mostly positive, with the main potential trade-offs connected to land competition and food security. Forest projects should be conducted in light of the local context and community to be successful, and be developed together with measures that improve the efficiency in the agri-food sector at both local and global levels (e.g., closing yield gaps in developing countries, reducing beef consumption) to decrease pressure on land resources and reduce inequalities (Humpenöder et al., 2022). Forest-based solutions are relatively inexpensive and may enable distributional, recognitional and procedural equity, provided that identities, knowledge, values and views of local communities are considered (Erbaugh et al., 2020; Lenzi et al., 2021). There is evidence that reforestation programmes have helped to support local livelihoods and decrease poverty, but economic benefits are dependent on CO2 sequestration pricing schemes, support for nature conservation benefits and existence of national targets and/or private investments (Brauman et al., 2013; Heilmayr et al., 2020; Humpenöder et al., 2022; Ota et al., 2020). In cases where equity was not recognized or enhanced, the risks of suboptimal outcomes have been higher (Börner et al., 2020; Rantala et al., 2013; Schreckenberg et al., 2016). Social acceptability of forest-based options is usually higher in developed countries, where forests are regulated via certified practices of management and various levels of protection, while it tends to be lower in developing countries and remote areas that are highly dependent on wood supply for heating or cooking (Paletto et al., 2013; Purnomo et al., 2005). Participatory processes, education and transfer of rights to local communities can contribute to procedural equity and challenge power imbalances (Chandra & Mukhopadhyay, 2022; Karsenty & Salau, 2023; Nantongo et al., 2019; Sadowska, 2022). More generally, community forest management in developing countries is a viable model for sustainable forestry, carbon sequestration and livelihoods (Apipoonyanon et al., 2020; Charnley et al., 2022). These activities benefit from being implemented by prioritizing local communities’ rights to manage and restore forests (Erbaugh et al., 2020). The implementation may require financial and technological support to minimize trade-offs between socio-economic and environmental outcomes, with active consideration of gender dynamics (Karsenty & Salau, 2023; Sheppard et al., 2020). INCLUDING RELEVANT ASPECTS OF THE ENERGY SYSTEM

title: Efficient water use in agriculture
definition: Efficient water use in agriculture (both water quantity and quality) can be implemented by planting drought resistant crops, optimizing fertilizer use, and practices such as conservation agriculture (Hobbs et al., 2008; Pittelkow et al., 2015) and can be used to alleviate water scarcity and food insecurity (Blum, 2005; Ruggiero et al., 2017; Sivamani et al., 2000; Tilman et al., 2001) and improve water quality, human health and biodiversity (Darch et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2017; Humbert et al., 2016; Jwaideh et al., 2022; Tilman et al., 2001). There is well established evidence to show that optimizing fertilizer application reduces chemicals in water and thus increases water quality, and the respective economic costs and benefits have been extensively studied (e.g., Garcia-Hernandez et al., 2022; Lötjönen & Ollikainen, 2019; Sihvonen et al., 2021). The benefits of implementation of this response option vary locally (Mbava et al., 2020; Molden et al., 2010), with the most pressing areas being water-scarce regions (Vishwanathan et al., 2021), where 25 per cent of the global population lives (WWAP, 2015). Efficient water use in crop production, which can be achieved through drought-resistant crops, is also one of the 10 science-based policy recommendations for agriculture (Garibaldi et al., 2019). However, the temporal scale is short because crops are grown annually and fertilizer is often applied annually or more frequently. In contrast, long-term fertilizer application may have effects on human health that are not observed over shorter time periods (Chen et al., 2020). Implementing this response option benefits water for both humans and ecosystems (Evans & Sadler, 2008), as it reduces competition for freshwater supplies (Chouchane et al., 2020) and improves water quality (Darch et al., 2014). Drought resistant crops can decrease farmers’ risks and increase crop yields and farm income (Birthal et al., 2012; Martey et al., 2020), while also providing food security by using underutilized crop species (Icka & Damo, 2023). There are also health benefits from naturally drought resistant plants in their contribution to pharmaceutical compounds (Gechev et al., 2014), and it is possible that the drought resistance as well as the quantity and quality of such compounds can be enhanced with plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (Vaghela & Gohel, 2023), or through fertilizer reduction that may reduce cancer and non-cancer disease risk by up to 21 per cent from changes in micronutrient (e.g., lead, zinc, copper) uptake (X.-X. Chen et al., 2020). The use of drought resistant crops can improve land management (e.g., Thierfelder et al., 2015) when aligned with conservation agriculture and land tenure rights (Kabubo-Mariara, 2007; Nguyen et al., 2023). Drought resistant crops can also reduce emissions of methane, and implementing optimal fertilizer application rates can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 20 per cent by 2050 (Gao & Cabrera Serrenho, 2023). The use of inorganic nitrogen fertilizer can disproportionally affect uneducated and poor women and children through increased morbidity and mortality by absorbing toxins from rice paddies where the fertilizer is used (Farnworth et al., 2017), and lack of a free market means some countries may impose tariffs that create economic inequities (Filippelli, 2018). Reducing the impacts of agriculture on water quality and quantity can free up water to be used for other uses and is also more cost-effective as fertilizer application rates are reduced to minimize runoff of fertilizers into water sources.

title: Reduce food loss and waste
definition: Globally, about one third of all produced food for human consumption is lost and wasted across the entire supply chain annually (Ishangulyyev et al., 2019). Such loss and waste are 1.3 billion tons per annum, equivalent to $1 trillion, and enough to feed more than double the number of undernourished people. Similarly, 8-10 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions are associated with food loss and waste (IPCC, 2019). Reducing food loss and waste (food loss and waste) can be applied from local to global levels in different production and post-harvest supply chains, with particularly strong impacts on climate change mitigation (global potential: 1.4-3.3 GtCO2e yr-1) (FAO, 2019b; Hayashi et al., 2022) and adaptation (1.26 billion people) (FAO, 2022a). Reducing food loss and waste can save up to 21 per cent of freshwater which could otherwise be used in growing food, or the equivalent of 21 m3 of freshwater per capita per year (Marston et al., 2021). Reducing food loss and waste has the potential to close the gap between food needed in 2050 and food available in 2010 by more than 20 per cent. It would avoid approximately 2.78 million km2 of intact land being converted to agriculture (Kummu, 2012). Halving food loss and waste reduces the global need for cropland area by around 14 per cent (IPCC, 2019). Reducing food loss and waste by 75 per cent could yield a 24 per cent decline in environmental pressures. If diets are optimized to reduce their environmental footprints, the pressure on cropland could be reduced by 50 per cent (Benton et al., 2021). There is also a risk that food loss and waste would increase due to a shift to sustainable healthy diets considering increased demand for more perishable foods; the land savings offered by reduced food loss and waste require strong governance measures, and complementary measures to reduce expansion of agricultural lands. Food loss and waste and public health intersect primarily in the domains of food security, food safety and nutrition, though it has no impact on food access or the nutritional value of food (Neff et al., 2015). The use of cold chain and packaging technologies, which can help reduce food loss and waste, increase energy and materials use in the food system (IPCC, 2019). There are no known social acceptability issues associated with reducing food loss and waste. Economic analyses propose that reducing 25 per cent of food loss and waste would yield a $455 billion economic benefit, with an investment cost of $30 billion per year to 2025, and creating $255 billion in business opportunities (FOLU, 2019). Reducing food loss and waste is strongly aligned with multiple international frameworks such as the SDGs (Champions, 2021), the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, Paris Agreement and United Nations Food Systems Pathways. Approaches that have been adopted at different contexts and scales to reduce food loss and waste include developing technologies and infrastructures, changing behaviour, enhancing food management skills (e.g., sorting, processing, cooking), developing protocols and legislation, and redistributing food (Nicastro & Carillo, 2021). Despite adopting different approaches, the SDG12.3 is woefully off-target. In order to achieve this target by 2030, many governments and businesses need to aggressively pursue the target-measure-act approach to reduce food waste, set a reduction target aligned with SDG target 12.3, measure food loss and waste to identify hot spots and monitor progress, and act more boldly to reduce food loss and waste (Champions, 2021).

title: Sustainable healthy diets*
definition: To be healthy, diets must meet four core principles driven by human biology and universal in their application. Specifically, healthy diets are adequate in essential nutrients, without excess, diverse in a variety of foods for various food groups, balanced in energy intake and sources, and moderate in the consumption of nutrients and foods associated with negative health outcomes. Shifting to healthy diets includes both increasing access to the diversity of culturally relevant under-consumed foods while significantly reducing unhealthy over-consumption, notably of sugar, salt and fat including red-meat, impacting nearly 2 billion adults today (González et al., 2020; Poore & Nemecek, 2018; Swinburn et al., 2019). Insufficient access to healthy diets is the most significant driver of premature mortality today affecting more than half of the global population and accounting for six of the top 11 risk factors driving the global burden of disease (Afshin et al., 2019). A shift to healthy diets (Willett, 2019) alone represents highly significant reduction in environmental pressure including a 29 per cent reduction in food-based GHG emissions and a 5-9 per cent reduction in other environmental impacts including reduced nutrient pollution, blue water consumption and land allocated to production. Shifts to healthy diets that also focus on sustainability could result in a 56 per cent reduction in food-based GHG emissions, with a 6-22 per cent reduction in other environmental factors without compromising health (Kim et al., 2020; Springmann et al., 2018). Impacts on biodiversity (Kastner et al., 2012) and climate change are dependent on policies and actions that halt the conversion of ecosystems of high ecological integrity. There are weaker effects on aquatic biodiversity which are more dependent on sustainable intensification, ecological intensification and reduced pollution. Shifts to healthy diets have weak impacts on water savings and may require additional freshwater for fruit, nut and vegetable production (Springmann et al., 2018). They also have weak effects on water quality, increasing dependencies on nutrient applications and pollution. Significant increases in diet-related non-communicable disease incidence have been observed in most countries, including where malnutrition is in decline (Afshin et al., 2019; Swinburn et al., 2019). Regionally adapted shifts to healthy diets would reduce 11 million premature deaths per year (Afshin et al., 2019; Springmann et al., 2018). Between food group diversity is particularly important to human health and nutrition (Lachat et al., 2018), while within food group diversity is important to individual and cultural food choices (Argumedo et al., 2020; Johns et al., 2013; Johns & Eyzaguirre, 2006; Khoury et al., 2014; Solomons, 2000) compatible with healthy diets. This emphasizes that crop and food diversity receive insufficient attention despite their significant impacts on nexus issues. Current food production is incompatible with healthy diets with significant underproduction of major food groups (Kc et al., 2018; Willett, 2019). Alignment would require increases in fruit and vegetable production (Mason-D’Croz et al., 2019) of 8.72 per cent yr-1 (Kc et al., 2018), and nut production by 150 per cent by 2050 (Willett, 2019), zero to minimal growth in cereal production (Kc et al., 2018), and significant global reductions in the production of ruminant meat independent of changes in meat production practices (Springmann et al., 2018; Willett, 2019). Shifts to healthy diets are amongst the most cost-effective food system response option available (Bodirsky, 2023; Ruggeri-Laderchi et al., 2024). Diet-related non-communicable diseases currently cost $11 trillion in health costs alone; this is marginally lower than the economic value of food estimated at $12 trillion annually(Ruggeri Laderchi et al., 2024). Several actions are possible. Aligning agricultural, trade and subsidy policies, as well as health policies and actions, to food-based dietary guidelines and public food procurement have significant potential (Damania et al., 2023; FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP and WHO, 2022; Springmann & Freund, 2022; Valencia et al., 2019). Consumer education and food health and sustainability labelling, alone or in combination, can guide consumer choice (Cecchini & Warin, 2016; Contreras-Manzano et al., 2022; Hawley et al., 2013; Julia & Hercberg, 2017; Taillie et al., 2021) while providing a common standard for food companies. However, these are insufficient as stand-alone interventions (Borgmeier & Westenhoefer, 2009). Healthy diets have been found to potentially contribute 70 per cent of the benefits of a comprehensive food system transformation through their direct impacts on health and their indirect impacts on production, including stemming pressures for land use change and promoting biodiversity. Sustainable healthy diets are necessary to stay within the Paris Agreement long-term global goal to limit the increase in global average temperature to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels (M. A. Clark et al., 2020) and GBF targets (Leclère et al., 2018). However, there is inadequate implementation of policies, programs and interventions – even those with proven efficacy – with only limited spending going to improving nutrition by national governments in their own countries and by international development organizations (Global Nutrition Report, 2022).

title: Sustainable use of medicinal plants
definition: Traditional and complementary medicines usage is reported by 88 per cent of WHO member states (WHO, 2019c) and an estimated 4 billion people (IPBES, 2019a) across all countries critically rely on wild flora and fauna sourced medicines. Between 50,000-70,000 medicinal plants are used globally (Schippmann et al., 2006): 35,407 species have well-documented use (MPNS, 2023), 3,000 species are globally traded and 60-90 per cent are sourced from the wild with high risk of overextraction (Schindler, 2022). While IPLC hold extensive associated knowledge of health and nutrition (ECOSOC, 2023) inherently linked to their diverse socioecological systems, there is also historically codified traditional medicinal plant knowledge that is well integrated and regulated within national health systems (e.g., Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine (Cragg & Newman, 2013)) that is driving significant global demand for wild resources (Astutik et al., 2019). This highlights the need for comprehensive assessments on medicinal plant sourcing, conservation, trade, cultivation status and usage patterns within the health sector (Chen et al., 2016). Promotion of sustainable harvest and use and conservation education among stakeholders is in progress. Strengthening the value chain and developing economic opportunities for dependent communities to facilitate integrated biodiversity planning can strengthen ecological stewardship among communities (Volenzo & Odiyo, 2020). Technological innovations for improving yield and quality of medicinal plants, identification of possible substitutes for endangered species and large-scale, in-situ and ex-situ conservation programs are also gaining recognition and application (Applequist et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2016; Kathe et al., 2010; Ved et al., 2020). Use of traditional and complementary medicines contributes to accessible healthcare, especially in regions where it is less developed. Some phytochemicals and traditional therapies have a potential role in treating neglected tropical diseases such as leishmaniasis (Chouhan et al., 2014; Gutiérrez-Rebolledo et al., 2017; Iwu et al., 1994; Simoben et al., 2018), trypanosomiasis (Simoben et al., 2018), filariasis (Komoreng et al., 2017; Narahari et al., 2013, 2023), chikungunya (Bhakat & Soliman, 2015), helminthiasis (Cock et al., 2018; Romero-Benavides et al., 2017); malaria (Bekono et al., 2020; Willcox & Bodeker, 2004), non-communicable diseases (Howes et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2022) and mental well-being (Fajemiroye et al., 2016; Pferschy-Wenzig et al., 2022; Saki et al., 2014). Medicinal plants continue to be a source of bioactive leads and effective drug development and hold potential with novel methods (Cragg & Newman, 2013). Integrated research on potential health benefits, quality, safety and sustainable use need to be expanded (IPBES, 2022c) and the recently established WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre has a strategic plan to support evidence synthesis and research on these traditional medicinal practices globally. Implementation of free, prior and informed consent and appropriate mechanisms to assure equity for traditional knowledge holders in compliance with the Nagoya protocol requires ongoing attention. Climate change and biodiversity loss have created significant impact on the present and future availability and quality of medicinal plants (Applequist et al., 2020; Borrell et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2019). Climate migration can also reduce access to these resources (Pörtner et al., 2021). Medicinal plants can contribute to healthy food due to their rich sources of health-promoting ingredients (Jiang et al., 2021; Leakey et al., 2022). Agro-biodiversity systems such as homestead gardens can improve access to these plants (Mitra et al., 2020; Pörtner et al., 2021; M. Santos et al., 2022; Ved et al., 2020). A significant portion of medicinal plants are aquatic or semi-aquatic (Aasim et al., 2019; Arya et al., 2022; M. A. Butt et al., 2021); water stress can impact on availability of secondary metabolites (Netshiluvhi & Eloff, 2016; Noreen et al., 2022; Prinsloo & Nogemane, 2018), while contaminated water can lead to uptake of toxic substances (Sarma et al., 2011). This response option can enhance nature’s contributions to people and conservation targets (Barata et al., 2016; Kassam et al., 2010; Kathe et al., 2010; Unnikrishnan & Suneetha, 2012; Ved et al., 2020), but may also result in unsustainable use (IPBES, 2022c; Sharma & Kala, 2018). Medicinal plant and biofuel cultivation may have negative impacts on food production (Brahmanand et al., 2013). Conservation and sustainable use management (Barata et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016; Sharma & Kala, 2018)), increased cultivation (Brinckmann et al., 2022; Falco et al., 2020) and landscape restoration programs (Prasad et al., 2023) show indications of positive impact on the status of medicinal plants as well as nexus elements. For example, the National Medicinal Plants Board of the Government of India supports in-situ conservation, research and education across the country with 110 medicinal plants conservation areas with ex-situ conservation within medicinal plant conservation parks (Ved et al., 2020). Seventy-two medicinal plant conservation development areas have more recently focused on community engagement and opportunities for alternative livelihoods, such as through enrichment of existing farming systems and integration of medicinal plants with joint forest management (Biswas et al., 2017). As 90 per cent of medicinal plant species in India occur in forests, appropriate governance and multistakeholder partnerships between the Department of Forestry, research organizations and communities are key to successful implementation (Ved et al., 2020).

title: Reduce meat overconsumption
definition: Reducing overconsumption of red and processed meat is a globally applicable response option wherever overconsumption takes place.
