Currently, health recommendations vary between 98-500g (cooked) lean red meat/week for adults and little or no processed meat (WHO, 2023c). The associated burden of disease and recommended intake continue to be revised (Murray, 2022; WHO, 2023c) with variation between studies related to specific health risks and reference populations (e.g., Afshin et al., 2019; González et al., 2020; Papier et al., 2021). Moderating consumption of red meat has synergies with other nexus elements, particularly climate change and biodiversity, with few trade-offs. The response option recognises that undernutrition associated with underconsumption (including for meat-associated iron, B12 and zinc, and protein) persists in many populations (WHO, 2023c). The highest overconsumption of red meat occurs in high-income Australasia, North America, western Europe and southern and tropical Latin America, with 2.1 to 2.8 times

title: Offshore wind power
definition: Offshore wind energy is becoming a widely used solution for the decarbonization of the energy system. Its mitigation potential has been estimated at a maximum of 10 GtCO2/ yr by 2050 and from 0.3-0.8 ºC by 2100 (Barthelmie & Pryor, 2021; Pek, 2020). Offshore wind farms employ fixed-foundation or floating turbines. The latter can be placed in deeper waters and are less impactful, but knowledge gaps exist (Dorrell et al., 2022). Offshore wind farms negative environmental impacts, such as noise, contaminants, electromagnetic fields, and risk of collision and entanglement, with particularly detrimental effects on migrating birds and bats, seabirds, marine mammals, reptiles and on seabed habitats and sedimentary processes, and they could also facilitate species invasions (Dannheim et al., 2020; Galparsoro et al., 2022; Lloret et al., 2022; Saidur et al., 2011; Vaissière et al., 2014); though the same is true of fossil fuel infrastructure. Although biodiversity and water quality are negatively affected, these impacts are low when compared with those of other energy systems. Offshore wind farms can have positive impacts. The exclusion of trawling can contribute to biodiversity and conservation and even augment neighbouring fisheries (spillover effects). OWF also create artificial hard substrates that increase biodiversity (Ashley et al., 2014; Boutin et al., 2023; Degraer et al., 2020; Hammar et al., 2016), which increases carbon assimilation (Mavraki et al., 2020). Combining offshore wind farms with integrated multitrophic aquaculture is currently being explored (Banach et al., 2020; Buck et al., 2018; C.-T. Huang et al., 2022; Ingle et al., 2022; van den Burg et al., 2020), as an option to enhance food production. Optimal siting of offshore wind farms should minimize their negative effects (outside bird migration corridors) and maximize their positive benefits (homogeneous soft-bottoms) (Mavraki et al., 2020). Floating turbines can be used where possible. Ecosystem-based management principles are encouraged (Stelzenmüller et al., 2022; WWF, 2014) to avoid the not-in-my-backyard effect as seen in the Mediterranean Sea (Lloret et al., 2022) and minimize the detrimental effects on well-being. While operating offshore wind farms can be regarded as a renewable energy, the construction of the turbines and decommissioning phases currently require fossil fuels. Despite the drop in costs of this technology (Wiser et al., 2021), there is a risk that large parts of the globe lag behind unless transitional costs in developing countries are addressed. Recycling and circular (at least spiral) economy principles would help to improve sustainability, e.g., replacing critical components by common and/or renewable materials, reusing rare earth elements (Valero et al., 2018) or increasing the lifespan of turbines. Deep-sea mining to meet this demand, thereby impacting pristine marine areas, could have adverse consequences for biodiversity (Levin et al., 2020).

title: Solar photovoltaics on land
definition: Utility-scale solar energy installations (solar farms) to produce electricity by photovoltaics are among the most important options to produce renewable energy and mitigate climate change (Clarke et al., 2022), with estimates of global mitigation potentials up to 7 GtCO2/yr (Babiker et al., 2022) and specific primary energy yields ranging from about 600 to 3000 GJ per ha (Leirpoll et al., 2021). Solar PV can be deployed in different environments, from ground-mounted panels in rural areas to panels integrated into the built environment. Solar energy is key for improving adaptation capacity to climate change of local communities, as it secures an off-grid energy access (especially roof-top solar PV) (Schipper et al., 2022). Solar photovoltaics interact with all nexus elements, in both positive and negative ways. The main sustainability trade-offs of solar energy are connected to the possible competition with agricultural land, but these risks are reduced when solar panels are deployed on contaminated areas or over building/infrastructure roofs. Agro-photovoltaics, i.e., elevated PV panels in agricultural land that provide shading to the crops beneath them to preserve soil moisture and reduce drought stress, are an adaptation-mitigation strategy that can reduce the trade-offs associated with land use competition (Barron-Gafford et al., 2019). A potential large-scale deployment of photovoltaic solar farms in a relatively limited area (e.g., over the Sahara Desert) has the potential to impact global cloud cover formation, precipitation patterns and increase surface temperature through disturbed atmospheric teleconnections induced by changes in biophysical surface properties (Long et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2021; Barron-Gafford et al., 2016). Off-grid and small-scale photovoltaic systems have the highest levels of social acceptance among renewables (Cousse, 2021; Patel & Rao, 2016). Although it might have high infrastructure costs for households, supporting policies (tax credits, installation subsidies, etc.) and long-term extra earnings make micro-and small-scale applications affordable (O’Shaughnessy, 2022; O’Shaughnessy et al., 2020), even for remote regions in developing economies where PV systems can enable basic rights, such as electricity access and promotion of education, emergency healthcare and early-warnings of natural disasters (Borenstein, 2017; Dholakia, 2018; Moner-Girona et al., 2021).

title: Sustainable bioeconomy
definition: Circular bioeconomy is an innovative concept that combines the principles of circular economy and bioeconomy to harness renewable natural capital, including biological resources for economic, environmental and social benefits. Circular bioeconomy contributes to several crucial outcomes across different sectors. It protects ecosystems and environmental integrity, prevents Nexus element Positive interactions Negative interactions Climate change High climate change mitigation and adaptation potential (see text). Large-scale deployment in a limited area risks altering moisture circulation pathways and inducing other climate feedbacks (e. g., changes in surface and cloud albedo) (Y. Li et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2021). Biodiversity The humid micro-habitat that forms underneath solar panels favour the presence of various invertebrates, pollinators and insects (M. Graham et al., 2021; Nordberg et al., 2021). Installation of solar farms on land has been associated with a degradation of natural habitats, habitat fragmentation and disorientation/damages of wildlife species because of the atypical sunlight or infrastructure concentration (Moscatelli et al., 2022; Szabadi et al., 2023). These negative effects can be mitigated through a variety of measures, such as revegetating areas between and under the rows of solar panels (Bennun et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2023). Water When deployed on land, solar PV offers drought resilience and groundwater sustainability, as it preserves soil humidity, and the water consumption of solar farms is one of the lowest among the different renewable energy alternatives (much lower than that of thermal power plants) (He et al., 2019; Macknick et al., 2012). The water needs to clean solar panels that are exposed to dust in arid regions can increase competition for water with other uses, especially in areas affected by water scarcity (Dahlioui et al., 2022; Supe et al., 2024). Food The use of solar energy in food processing in remote rural settings near the harvest site supports delivery of quality food at low cost, as it improves options for transportation and storage (e. g., enhancing refrigeration, drying or ventilation) and reduces post-harvest food losses (Barisik Marasli et al., 2022; Eswara & Ramakrishnarao, 2013). The main food system impacts of solar energy are connected to the possible competition with agricultural land, as PV panels can replace food crops and induce market-mediated effects (Capellán-Pérez et al., 2017; Miskin et al., 2019). These risks do not occur when solar panels are integrated within urban systems, but their climate change mitigation potential is lower (Yeligeti et al., 2023). Health Solar energy can induce benefits to human health by reducing air pollution relative to thermal plants and by securing electricity access for health facilities in poor and/or remote areas (Adair-Rohani et al., 2013; Dholakia, 2018; Roy et al., 2018). A proper disposal of solar panels is necessary when plants are decommissioned to avoid chemical pollution to the environment and exposure to carcinogenic gases (Dhar et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2021). INCLUDING RELEVANT ASPECTS OF THE ENERGY SYSTEM biodiversity loss, minimizes natural resource consumption, reduces pollution and GHG emissions, and promotes sustainable management of biological resources. Reducing the use of pesticides and fertilizers, improving soil health and water quality, and promoting habitat connectivity positively influence biodiversity. Investments in circular bioeconomy can also contribute up to 200 MtCO2/yr of sequestration by 2050 (Gomez San Juan et al., 2022; Stegmann et al., 2022). A circular bioeconomy improves water quality and quantity by implementing bio-based products, water recycling and water-efficient measures in agriculture and industry. It addresses issues such as agricultural runoff, water efficiency, advanced wastewater treatment and wetland restoration (Morseletto et al., 2022; Rodríguez-Espinosa et al., 2023; Rosenboom et al., 2022; Sauvé et al., 2021; Schneider et al., 2021). In terms of food production, a circular bioeconomy focuses on reducing food waste, developing technologies for food waste recycling, lowering food prices, improving nutrition and diversifying food supply through unconventional sources. It optimizes resource utilization and waste reduction, and encourages sustainable practices using breeding technologies, bio-based products and energy, including energy from waste, resulting in improved environmental performance (Gomez San Juan et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2021; Trigo et al., 2023). Examples of circular bioeconomy are found in many countries. While the circular bioeconomy approach can align with socio-cultural values by integrating ILK, respecting cultural diversity and involving stakeholders, concerns have been raised regarding its effectiveness in decoupling economic development from finite resource consumption. Proactive risk management strategies and policy frameworks are essential to ensure long-term success and sustainability. Equity should also be prioritized by acknowledging and respecting the diverse identities, knowledge systems, world views and values of communities and stakeholders (Bastos Lima & Palme, 2022; Giampietro, 2019; Ncube et al., 2022; Padilla-Rivera et al., 2020). A circular bioeconomy aids in the conservation of terrestrial, inland water and marine ecosystems, mitigates climate change, reduces poverty and improves health and well-being (Fraga-Corral et al., 2022; Gomez San Juan et al., 2022; Stephenson & Damerell, 2022). Thus, the circular bioeconomy approach offers a promising approach to address environmental, economic and social challenges while promoting sustainable development and biodiversity conservation. title: Manage wastewater
definition: Wastewater pollution, including excessive fertilizer use, can be reduced by repositioning wastewater management from an end-of-pipe problem to a circular economy opportunity which treats wastewater as a renewable resource to be conserved and sustainably managed (Hdidou et al., 2022). Sustainable sanitation practices play a crucial role in addressing the interconnected challenges of water availability, biodiversity conservation and climate actions (Hutton & Chase, 2016). Safe and appropriate wastewater management has potential co-benefits such as improved ecosystem health, human health and well-being, reduced dependence on synthetic fertilizers and economic opportunities (UNEP, 2023). Actions include: (a) reducing the volume of wastewater produced; (b) preventing and reducing water contamination; and (c) sustainably managing wastewater for resource recovery and reuse. Several solutions exist for the collection and treatment of wastewater to recover resources (such as nutrients) of appropriate quality standards depending on intended end use (UNEP, 2023; WWAP, 2015). Access to adequate sanitation services and domestic wastewater treatment is a critical issue in several parts of Latin American, Asian and African countries. Hence, sanitation projects implemented in these regions are applying ecological sanitation approaches for the recovery of resources like biogas, struvite, carbon dioxide and clean water from domestic wastewater to ‘close the loop’ (Werkneh & Gebru, 2023). Implementing such approaches has many benefits for the nexus elements. Wetlands, both natural and constructed, are a nature-based solution that can remove nutrients, reduce maintenance costs and energy consumption, and provide wastewater reuse and application of biosolids in agriculture (Amorim Junior et al., 2021; Hdidou et al., 2022; Oliveira et al., 2021). For example, plants from constructed wetlands can be used for biofuel and can reduce cooking fuel by up to 55 per cent (Avellán & Gremillion, 2019). Preventing contamination of drinking water sources, such as aquifers and surface waters, from wastewater is key to ensuring the quality of water resources, providing benefits to biodiversity and improving human health by reducing diseases such as diarrhoeal illness (Fewtrell et al., 2005). Improved sanitation also saves lives and facilitates economic growth (Murungi & van Dijk, 2014; Van Minh & Hung, 2011). Wastewater management is also pitched as an important component of One Health, especially for challenges such as antibiotic resistance (Gholizadeh et al., 2023; Rousham et al., 2018), and addressing marine pollution (Shuval, 2003). Enhancing the sustainability of sanitation projects entails co-designing and co-managing facilities with communities to invoke a sense of ownership, educating users with proper hygiene maintenance and building capacities to regulate the flow and treatment of wastewater (Brands, 2014) as well as developing effective business models (Amoah et al., 2021; Taron et al., 2023). To address the existing institutional and financial fragmentation in the provision of sanitation, comprehensive and integrated policies supported by cooperative and participatory methods are needed (Loewenson et al., 2023). Closing the funding gap in sanitation calls for specialized cross-sectoral nodal entities or the convergence of efforts across ministries to produce significant sanitation results. For example, the African Water Facility supports governments in the implementation of several water supply and sanitation projects in sub-Saharan Africa (GBAD, 2020). The circular economy appears to be an effective model for sanitation because it focuses on the entire sanitation chain, which includes the provision of toilets, waste collection, treatment and transformation into by-products (Guerra-Rodríguez et al., 2020; Mallory et al., 2020; Smol et al., 2020). Reusing water in agriculture can help with irrigation, increase agricultural yield and even extend the growing season, while also lowering the danger of drought for crops. Wastewater and agricultural inputs can be used for any kind of crop, depending on the treatment standard and the procedures followed (Hanjra et al., 2012). Farmers in low-income countries have cited the year-round availability of wastewater as a significant reason in favour of its reuse (Drechsel et al., 2010). Systems that assure wastewater treatment prior to discharge mitigate risks to ecosystems and nature’s contributions to people. These include enhancing freshwater quality and safety, which makes it more usable, and lowering pollution and eutrophication in food-producing ecosystems (Corcoran et al., 2010). Significant amounts of nutrients can be recovered from wastewater and excreta; estimates suggest that all current fertilizer use in smallholder-dominated countries could theoretically be replaced with nutrients recovered from human excreta (Rosemarin et al., 2008). The 330 km3 of municipal wastewater generated every year worldwide could theoretically irrigate around 15 per cent of all currently irrigated crops (Mateo-Sagasta et al., 2015). The primary organic matter found in excreta and wastewater is composed of lipids, carbs and proteins, which can be used as a soil conditioner which would address declining soil quality. This is especially true if it is combined with food waste and agricultural leftovers (Lal, 2008). Additionally, improving soil organic matter content reduces the impacts of run-off and eutrophication issues by enhancing nutrient and water retention (Renwick et al., 2021). Efficiently producing renewable energy from wastewater and excreta can also be a successful strategy for mitigating the effects of climate change (Hanjra et al., 2012). Enhancing sanitation and managing wastewater can significantly aid in mitigating climate change by decreasing emissions of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, as the waste sector contributes significantly to global emissions. Producing biogas is an effective approach to extract the energy from these waste streams and the most compatible with resource recovery (Werkneh & Gebru, 2023). It can also be an inexpensive and healthier substitute for wood and other biomass fuels used by low-income households (Rajendran et al., 2012). The estimated 330 km3 of municipal wastewater output could theoretically supply electricity for almost 130 million people based on an average yearly electricity usage of 3,500 kWh/household (Mateo-Sagasta et al., 2015). The controlled burning or incineration of waste streams is another method of extracting energy, which is prevalent in Sweden and Denmark; China is also making significant investments in the incineration of solid waste (Li et al., 2015). For example, changing the treatment design in a more traditional wastewater management system can cut carbon dioxide emissions by 35 per cent (Khiewwijit et al., 2015). Therefore, recovering energy from excreta, wastewater and other organic waste and making treatment systems efficient can aid in increasing access to contemporary energy while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Reduce nutrient pollution
definition: Feeding the world while reducing nutrient pollution can be applied at the global scale, requiring nutrient use efficiencies between 60 and 77 per cent. Reductions can be prioritized in regions where intensive agriculture is pervasive with increased nutrient use in regions where productivity remains low (Schulte-Uebbing et al., 2022). Reducing nutrient use is beneficial to overall environmental performance but can result in lower yields, although the evidence for this relationship is weak (Bijay-Singh & Craswell, 2021; Nadeem et al., 2022). Reducing nutrient pollution has strong benefits for reducing the risk of contamination of surface water used for human consumption, preserving water quality for humans and ecosystems, and decreasing overall environmental exposure to algal blooms (Jarvie et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021; Rastogi et al., 2015). It also benefits human health as cyanobacterial blooms and the accumulation of several cyanotoxins in water bodies pose a severe risk to global public health and aquatic organisms (Rastogi et al., 2015). Algal blooms have been associated with several water-borne diseases (e.g., cholera) (Epstein, 1993) and other morbidities including neurological disorders (Schleyer & Vardi, 2020). Reducing nutrient pollution has positive outcomes for native biodiversity and ecological functions, although evidence is weak. Actions such as improved nutrient use efficiency, precision application and creating effective buffers between agricultural systems and adjacent aquatic systems could have net positive impacts on terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity, while simultaneously creating habitat and connectivity (Asbjornsen et al., 2014; L. J. Cole et al., 2020; Fremier et al., 2015). Reducing nutrient pollution has minimal impacts on climate change, as the reduction in nutrient application to reduce pollution in intensive agricultural areas is nearly equal to the increases required to close yield gaps in areas where productivity is low (Schulte-Uebbing et al., 2022). Nevertheless, 15 per cent of global fossil fuel use is for creating nutrient inputs for food (GAFF, 2023). Public opinion is generally supportive of reducing nutrient pollution. However, farmers’ perspectives may be less supportive due to tension between nutrients as an important agricultural input and a pollutant (Kanter et al., 2020; Rauh & Hughes, 2023). Reduced nutrient use is associated with reduced yield risks, but also with improved nutrient use efficiencies for which investment in advanced technologies is required (Finger et al., 2019; Mizik, 2023; Rossi et al., 2023). Normative tools providing a locally adaptable framework and a voluntary set of practices to guide different stakeholders directly or indirectly involved with fertilizer use and management can play a significant role in reducing nutrient pollution (e.g., the International Code of Conduct for the Sustainable Use and Management of Fertilizers (FAO, 2019a). All these options have an impact on reducing both nitrogen and phosphorus pollution (Springmann et al., 2018). However, implementation at scale is very costly and often limited (S. Kumar et al., 2020; Mizik, 2023). The efficacy of actions is often dependent on agricultural systems, climate, soil types, topography and the nutrient management approaches employed (Liu et al., 2021).

title: Reduce pesticide pollution
definition: Reducing pesticide pollution can be applied globally but should be prioritized in geographic areas with large areas under intensive agriculture where pollution risks are high (FAO, 2023b). Ten percent of the 3 million tonnes of pesticides used annually in agriculture remains in the upper soil horizons as residue, 7 per cent leaches into the aquifers and 0.1 per cent enters rivers and oceans (Maggi et al., 2019). These residues put 64 per cent of agricultural land at risk of pollution and 31 per cent at high risk of pollution (Tang et al., 2022). Biocides residues have a wide spectrum of half-life and cycle and can persist in the environment as pollutants over the medium to long-term (UNEP, 2001). Reducing pesticide pollution has very high benefits for reducing surface and groundwater pollution (Maggi et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2022), preserving water quality for humans and ecosystems and decreasing overall environmental exposure to persistent pesticides (UNEP, 2001). Reducing pesticide residues in the environment also benefits soil biodiversity that is essential for maintaining soil health and performance (Maggi & Tang, 2021; Relyea, 2005) – notably carbon storage (Bastida et al., 2021; Patel et al., 2022). However, in the absence of alternative pest management practices, reducing pesticide use may decrease yield protection efficiency and increase costs (Ahvo et al., 2023). Decreasing pesticide transport via surface water and wind drift to non-treated land (Desmarteau et al., 2020; Maggi et al., 2023) can have positive effects on preserving native biodiversity in protected areas and the wider landscape. This can improve associated ecological functions, which in turn can preserve/improve ecosystem resilience capability (Beaumelle et al., 2023; Zikankuba et al., 2019). Riparian buffers are useful for reducing pesticide flow into freshwater systems, which have important climate and biodiversity co-benefits (Asbjornsen et al., 2014). However, similar to reducing nutrient pollution, there is currently no evidence of the impact of reducing pesticide pollution on climate change, although an estimated 15 per cent of global fossil fuel use is allocated to agricultural inputs including pesticides (GAFF, 2023). The response option is highly beneficial to human health as pesticide residues are present in fresh and processed foods, leading to toxicological risks (Boobis et al., 2008). Documented evidence shows that reducing pesticide use decreases environmental loads of residues and potential human exposure to them (Maggi et al., 2021). This in turn decreases the associated burden of diseases (Landrigan et al., 2018), as well as pesticide application operators’ consciousness of exposure risk and associated mental well-being (Daghagh Yazd et al., 2019). While social acceptability of the response option is high, alignment to political agendas is intermediate to low mainly due to industrial assets, intellectual property and trading balance in imports/exports of individual countries (Tang et al., 2022). In contrast, technical feasibility is well developed by means of a number of alternatives including integrated pest management as organic farming (Baker et al., 2020), biological pest control (Lucchi & Benelli, 2018; T. Williams et al., 2013), precision farming (Finger et al., 2019; Shamshiri et al., 2018) and protected farming (Van Lenteren, 2000), although there are some limitations on their application at scales and associated costs (Deguine et al., 2021). Normative tools providing a framework that guides government regulators, the private sector, civil society and other stakeholders on best practice in managing pesticides throughout their lifecycle can play a significant role in reducing pesticide pollution (FAO & WHO, 2014).

title: Reduce plastic pollution
definition: Reducing plastic pollution as a response option can be applied globally given the threat it poses to nexus elements notably, water (Barcelo & Pico, 2020; Borrelle et al., 2020; R. Kumar et al., 2021; Mbachu et al., 2021). Growing demand for food and food convenience, while increasing food safety and reducing food loss and waste, has increased food packaging, including single-use plastics (Geyer, 2020; Ncube et al., 2021; A. T. Williams & Rangel-Buitrago, 2022). Plastics can accumulate and persist in the environment for several decades, requiring short to prolonged impact mitigation strategies (Yao et al., 2022). Reducing plastic pollution has several impacts on the nexus elements. It can reduce access to healthy food, and reductions in plastic packaging for perishable foods can lower their shelf life reducing availability and increasing food waste. These impacts may be higher than the detrimental impacts of plastics although there is currently low confidence and high uncertainty in these numbers (White & Lockyer, 2020). Implementation of measures to reduce single-use plastics directly reduce plastic waste in water courses and hence improves water quality (Kiessling et al., 2023), which has positive impacts on wildlife (Puskic et al., 2020) and added benefits of reducing flood risk from blocked sewage systems. There is also good evidence that reducing plastic waste in soils improves soil quality (by reducing soil bulk density and improving soil porosity and hydraulic conductivity), resulting in higher yields (Koskei et al., 2021; Shah & Wu, 2020). For example, shifting from use of plastic mulch to biodegradable mulch in farming can reduce plastic residue accumulation in soils, with numerous environmental benefits including enhanced food production (Koskei et al., 2021; Shah & Wu, 2020). A higher percentage of recycled plastic content could reduce health risks, resulting in ‘longer human life per tonne of plastic recycled’ (Deeney et al., 2022). In addition, reducing plastic pollution is associated with reduced exposure to carcinogenic or endocrine disrupting chemicals (Revel et al., 2018; M. Smith et al., 2018). Reducing plastic pollution through substitutes and recycling are socially acceptable but there are geographical disparities and information gaps and the cost of alternatives can preclude change (Ciano et al., 2023; Filho et al., 2021; Oke et al., 2020). Political will to reduce pollution from plastics broadly exists but implementation is often problematic. Bans of single-use plastics have not been effective in some countries, and subsidizing recycling often requires costly government intervention (Ogutu et al., 2023; Raab et al., 2023; Williams & Rangel-buitrago, 2022). There is limited evidence of increased costs to consumers from novel packaging materials (Ciano et al., 2023). There are high production costs associated with shifting from use of plastics in the food system yet the economic, social and environmental performance of biodegradable plastics is relatively low and uncertain (Moshood et al., 2022). Depending on specific interventions, technical feasibility varies. Substitution of plastics (e.g., edible films and coatings) are still in less advanced stages and could create leakage to raw materials (e.g., wood and crops). Although policy-based options are better developed, such as those guided by biodegradable and compostable plastic product standards (FAO, 2021), they are weakly implemented or in a piecemeal manner at best (Shah & Wu, 2020).

title: Pollution prevention
definition: Health risks from pollution (air, water and soil) are influenced by anthropogenic actions including human induced pollution, dietary and consumption behaviour, unregulated economic growth, industrialization and demographics (P. Dasgupta et al., 2018; FAO & UNEP, 2021; Thompson & Darwish, 2019). Estimates indicate that 9 million premature deaths occur per year from pollution, of which 90 per cent are in lower-middle-income countries and among vulnerable populations, with variation in attributable sources of pollution (Fuller et al., 2022) and in disease burdens within regions and countries (WHO, 2019a; J. Wolf et al., 2023). There are multiple benefits to other nexus elements by linking pollution prevention and health protection. Reductions in indoor and ambient air pollution, biomass consumption, and air-water-chemical pollution-induced habitat and biodiversity loss can enhance access to safe water and clean air, enhance sustainable food production and food and nutritional security (Willett et al., 2019; Woldetsadik et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2019) and avoid the emergence of diseases (Aerts et al., 2018; Maquart et al., 2022; Marselle et al., 2021; Schmeller et al., 2018; Willetts et al., 2023). Several interconnections exist between climate change, biodiversity and pollution management for advancing human well-being (Akinnawo, 2023; Boudewijns et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021; Zahno et al., 2020). Examples include the sustainable use of medicinal plants and reducing pollution within the health and care sectors through reduced emissions and residues, promotion of clean energy, green infrastructure and aligned procurement policies (Green Deal, 2023; Lenzen et al., 2020) (WHO, 2023a). Reducing pollution was also assessed by other subchapters of. Actions to benefit health and other nexus elements includes labelling of both nutritional and environmental outcomes for promoting healthy diets (De Bauw et al., 2021); command and control instruments such as bans (e.g., for plastic pollution); impact evaluations to trigger response options such as water pollution treatment for reducing morbidity (Luo et al., 2022) and air pollution reduction for increasing life expectancy in lower-middle-income countries (Abbasi-Kangevari et al., 2023); reducing harm from noise and air pollution by increased exposure to biodiversity (Marselle et al., 2021); and lowering risks of mortality and morbidity from air pollution reduction through green areas (Bloemsma et al., 2019; Crouse et al., 2019). Solutions for pollution may come with economic costs, including those borne by individuals (e.g., through temporary job losses in response to changing technologies), public or private entities (e.g., losses from closure of thermal power plants), and governments (e.g., costs of funding transitions to net zero or changing land use in favour of conservation). This deters action even where cost-effective technologies are available (e.g., improved cookstoves, clean cooking fuels, greening infrastructural interventions, tackling short-lived climate pollutants and waste treatment in healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors) (Eckelman et al., 2020; Lenzen et al., 2020; Speight, 2020). The high social costs of pollution (e.g., lowered labour productivity, morbidity, mortality, opportunity costs from diversion of public resources, including finance and human resources to deal with the consequences for healthcare) and the fact that markets fail to convey these costs to society, calls for publicly supported actions for pollution prevention. The social costs of inaction are usually much higher than the costs of prevention (World Bank, 2016). While restoration is costlier than conservation for both ecosystems and human health (P. Dasgupta, 2021), there is evidence that the health co-benefits to humans and nature from climate change mitigation, inclusive of air pollution reduction, are greater than the costs of such policies (M. A. Martin et al., 2022). Reducing pollution and improving health, supported by a judicious mix of regulatory, financial and social mechanisms, and supported by value systems, can be used to realize the social gains, internalize externalities and manage costs. For example, efforts to minimize land and water pollution have been initiated as actions to enhance relational (nature for culture) values in parts of the Hindu Kush Himalaya (P. Dasgupta & Shakya, 2023). Health actors can engage in evidence generation, management and co-creation of integrated public policies influencing funding, social behaviour and legal instruments to prevent pollution. Pollution reduction is key to achieving global goals and targets on health as enshrined in the SDGs, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and Paris Agreement (Baste & Watson, 2022). Reducing air pollution has transformative potential reaching across nexus elements, with the most immediate and significant benefits and co-benefits accruing to human health (Roy, 2018). title: Sustainable intensification*
definition: Sustainable intensification can be confused with other terms related to the sustainable production of food production. IPBES defines sustainable intensification as “a process or system where agricultural yields are increased without adverse environmental impact and without the conversion of additional non-agricultural land” (IPBES, 2016, 2018). Sustainable intensification can be applied globally on all arable and pastoral land due to yield gaps in many regions (Global Yield Gap and Water Productivity Atlas, n.d.) and has the potential to reduce environmental impacts while maintaining yields elsewhere (Halpern et al., 2022). It can be achieved through a wide range of approaches with differing impacts and timescales. Sustainable intensification has positive impacts across nexus elements. Yield-increasing response options; F03, Sustainable intensification; F04, Ecological intensification – croplands; F05 Ecological intensification – rangelands and F06 Ecological intensification – aquatic foods ) are needed to achieve these nexus benefits even if consumption changes; F11, Sustainable healthy diets ) are achieved (D. R. Williams et al., 2021). However, realizing benefits may require policy or economic mechanisms to avoid additional agricultural expansion (Desquilbet et al., 2017; Phalan et al., 2016). Sustainable intensification has limited the conversion of natural ecosystems avoiding up to 590 GtCO2e emissions from 1961-2005 (Burney et al., 2010). It is projected to reduce future emissions by 2-2.45 GtCO2e per year, largely through limiting agricultural expansion (M.A. Clark et al., 2020), and climate adaptation benefits achieved through sustainable intensification could impact up to 163 million people (P. Smith et al., 2020). Limiting agricultural expansion has also benefited biodiversity (Balmford, 2021) and future sustainable intensification could have huge benefits for native biodiversity and the area available for protection (Tilman et al., 2017; D. R. Williams et al., 2021), as well as off-farm benefits on ecological function, connectivity and resilience, while on-farm impacts vary depending on the approach (Ekroos et al., 2016; R. E. Green et al., 2005; Tscharntke et al., 2012). Sustainable intensification improves crop water-use efficiency, potentially reducing water use or producing more food for the same amount of water (Leakey et al., 2019; Wani et al., 2003). In livestock systems, it may increase blue and grey water use due to greater consumption of irrigated feeds (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012). It also increases water quality by reducing nutrient run-off and soil erosion (Z.-L. Cui et al., 2018; Finger et al., 2019). Sustainable intensification can have variable impacts on human health. Intensive livestock systems limit the probability of zoonotic disease spillover by reducing livestock-wildlife interactions, but may increase the probability of zoonotic disease take-off, antimicrobial resistance, foodborne diseases and air pollution (Gilbert et al., 2021; Post et al., 2020; Rohr et al., 2019). Interlinkages between sustainable intensification practices, air pollution and health are described in the case study in Box. Benefits through increased nutrition will only be realised if production is linked to sustainable healthy diets. title: Reduce short-lived climate pollutants
definition: Short‑lived climate pollutants are highly reactive compounds frequently co-emitted with CO2 in combustion processes for energy production or transport (Naik et al., 2021). They include aerosols, such as particulate matter (PM) or black carbon, sulphates (SOx), nitrates, ammonium (NH3), and ozone (O3) precursors such as nitrogen oxides (NOx) or volatile organic carbon. Short‑lived climate pollutants persist in the atmosphere from a few hours to a couple of months. Their climate effect predominantly occurs in the first two decades after emission (or formation) and consists of both warming and cooling, with potential changes in cloud formation and precipitation patterns (Bellouin et al., 2016; Bony et al., 2015; Naik et al., 2021). SLCPs are also the main contributors to air pollution, damaging human health and negatively influencing land and ocean ecosystem productivity with implications for food security, water quality and biodiversity (Silva et al., 2016; Stohl et al., 2015; Y. Xie et al., 2018). Emission sources and atmospheric concentrations of short‑lived climate pollutants are highly heterogenous. The largest surface concentrations of particulate matter occur in Southern Asia, Eastern Asia and the Middle East, where the dominant anthropogenic emission sources are biomass and coal fuel-based cooking and heating, and, especially in Eastern Asia, energy and industry (Naik et al., 2021). At a global scale, road transport emissions from gasoline and diesel vehicles are the dominant contributor to surface ozone concentrations in populated areas (Silva et al., 2016; Unger et al., 2020). Aviation is mostly responsible for emissions of NOx, aerosols and formation of persistent condensation trails (contrails) (Lee et al., 2021), while shipping is an important polluting factor (mainly SOx, NOx, and PM) in coastal areas along the major trade routes (Jonson et al., 2020; H. Liu et al., 2016). The type of short‑lived climate pollutant and impacts to be prioritized reflect the local context. For example, emissions from the residential and commercial sectors (fossil and biomass use for cooking and heating) and the energy sector (fossil fuel production, distribution and combustion) contribute the most to human exposure to PM, and mitigation measures in each region primarily target the main local source of pollution (i.e., the residential sector in Southern Asia and Africa, or the industry and energy sector in Central and Eastern Asia). Alternatively, emissions from energy and land transportation sectors contribute the most to ozone exposure and are relevant within cities affected by poor air quality. Short‑lived climate pollutant emission reduction strategies include measures such as energy efficiency, zero-emissions vehicles, reduced use of private vehicles, efficient and clean stoves for heating and cooking, soot filters, flue gas scrubbers and cleaner industrial processes. The interactions with nexus elements are multiple and complex. The evident and quantifiable health benefits of short‑lived climate pollutant abatement favor their social acceptance, but proper instruments should ensure a just transition, particularly when addressing the energy and transport sectors in poorer urban areas (Benmarhnia et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2016; Vandyck et al., 2018). Co-benefits for air quality and human health of short‑lived climate pollutant mitigation can offset the costs of climate measures (Harmsen et al., 2020; M. Li et al., 2018; Saari et al., 2015). The transformation of the energy system included in nationally determined contribution pledges following the Paris Agreement can reduce local air pollution and globally avoid 71 to 99,000 premature deaths annually by 2030 (1.5 million by 2050 under stricter mitigation scenarios), thereby offsetting the costs of climate policies (Vandyck et al., 2018). title: Integrated landscape and seascape approaches
definition: Integrated landscape and seascape approaches are comprehensive strategies to address the intricate interplay between socioeconomic and environmental objectives such as food production, local livelihoods, biodiversity conservation and climate action at landscape and seascape scales. Integrated landscape and seascape approaches encompass various frameworks including integrated landscape approaches (Reed et al., 2020), landscape stewardship (Bieling & Plieninger, 2017), foodscapes (Bossio et al., 2021), forest and landscape restoration (Chazdon et al., 2017), multifunctional scapes (Pörtner et al., 2021) and seascape approaches (Murphy et al., 2021). Integrated landscape and seascape approaches emphasize the integration of nexus elements across terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems and leverage various ecosystem-based approaches to address societal challenges (Cohen-Shacham et al., 2019). While the terminology may vary, the core concept revolves around holistic, long-term and adaptive management of landscapes and seascapes to achieve socioecological objectives through collaboration among stakeholders from different sectors and social groups (Reed et al., 2021). Integrated landscape and seascape approaches are a promising and well-practiced response option for the nexus as they operate across higher-order interactions (e.g., water-food-biodiversity, water-health-climate change) and place a particular emphasis on connectivity across socioecological land-and seascapes and the terrestrial, freshwater and marine realms (Nishi et al., 2022; Nishi & Yamazaki, 2020). Recent survey-based analysis suggests that highly integrated initiatives that include many sectors have an overall better performance for agriculture, nature conservation, livelihoods and effective governance in comparison to less integrated (siloed) initiatives which are biased towards conservation or agriculture (Carmenta et al., 2020). Integrated landscape and seascape approaches are implemented in all inhabited continents and include global scale programs such as the Satoyama Initiative, the UNESCO Man and Biosphere reserves and the FAO Globally Important Agriculture Heritage Systems, among others. Thirty integrated landscape and seascape approaches case studies were analysed in this subchapter: seven from Africa, twelve from the Americas, four from Asia and Oceania, and seven from Europe. This quantitative analysis was complemented by conclusions from global syntheses (Carmenta et al., 2020; Denier et al., 2015; Duncan et al., 2021; García-Martín et al., 2016; Suit et al., 2021). These diverse examples demonstrate the effectiveness of ILSA in benefitting multiple elements of the nexus and sustainability dimensions (ecological, social, and economic). Relative cost-effectiveness and affordability are also features that make integrated landscape and seascape approaches an attractive nexus response option (Arts et al., 2017). Integrated landscape and seascape approaches generally focus on food production and nature conservation as entry points, but also include and benefit water and climate change (Carmenta et al., 2020; Duncan et al., 2021; García-Martín et al., 2016; J. C. Milder et al., 2014; Obura et al., 2021), and health (Sakkhamduang et al., 2022), with most initiatives impacting three or more nexus elements. For example, the integrated landscape approach with IPLC engagement in decision making in Nagaland, India, strengthened and linked community conserved areas for conservation across three villages—Sukhai, Ghukhuyi, and Kivikhu—protecting 939 hectares (Edake et al., 2019). Hunting, tree felling, and destructive fishing were prohibited across the remaining forest and river landscapes. A capacity-building program reconnected the community with their forests, fostering conservation support through livelihood opportunities, such as ecotourism training, and involvement in biodiversity monitoring. The initiative revived the traditional practice of conserving community forests, secured by customary rights and reinforced by a joint management committee. Mobilization efforts and synergy-building enhanced nature’s contributions to people, improving productivity in shifting cultivation (jhum) areas. This outcome impacted all nexus elements though wildlife conservation and revival of wild populations, increased diversity; food from forest, restoration of food production; carbon storage in recovered/protected forest; traditional medicine secured and general wellbeing of community; enhanced watershed services of protected forest. The benefits of initiatives aimed at sustainable food production (JWRC, 2012; Karimova et al., 2022; Sasaoka, 2010) for improved terrestrial and coastal water quality (Déja et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2021; World Bank, 2021) and biodiversity conservation (Chape, 2015; Edake et al., 2020) are well documented. This is particularly visible at the landscape-seascape interface, where environmentally-friendly agricultural production activities upstream enhance plant and faunal diversity across the watershed and safeguard coastal and marine organisms and ecosystems (Guo et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Karimova & Lee, 2022; Tanaka et al., 2021; Turak et al., 2021). Synergies and trade-offs in relation to health and climate change (apart from disaster risk reduction) are much less reported in the literature. This may be explained by the difficulty of measuring and monitoring them within a short project span (two to three years) of most documented integrated landscape and seascape approaches (Nishi et al., 2021). title: Land and sea planning
definition: Land and sea planning (hereafter ‘planning’) is a technical-political-administrative process aimed to configure the use of terrestrial and marine territory in the long-term, considering potential and limitations of the area, aspirations of people and sustainable development objectives (Joanna, 2017; Massiris Cabeza, 2005). Marine spatial planning is now a key process within the current United Nations Decade of Ocean Research (Ehler, 2020; Kidd et al., 2020; Rivers et al., 2022). Planning is typically manifested through public policies, with a focus on developing medium-and long-term strategic plans and balancing trade-offs between multiple different uses of the natural environment (Lombard et al., 2019). The state plays a crucial role as a guarantor of territorial sustainability against multiple development pressures, within a process designed to be highly participatory and equitable, incorporating multi-stakeholder consultations and other tools (Sanabria Perez, 2014; Zaucha & Gee, 2019). A key outcome of planning is limiting accelerated urbanization by respecting natural and cultivated areas (Alfasi et al., 2012; Gurran et al., 2015). Thus, planning also conserves biodiversity and water, mitigates climate change and supports food production through agriculture, aquaculture and fisheries (Lombard et al., 2019; Rivers et al., 2022). Well implemented spatial plans also enhance human health and well-being through providing recreational access to natural environments (Day & Dobbs, 2013), and more recently meeting sociocultural needs (Saunders et al., 2019). Ninety examples of implementation of land planning examined7 showed regional differences. In Latin America, planning emphasized social and cultural aspects, serving as a tool for communities to protect their identities and rights linked to the territory (Asher & Ojeda, 2009). Elsewhere, land planning tends to be more technical, focusing on zoning of uses and achieving pre-established objectives, with less consideration of social and cultural aspects. However, recent sea planning cases now include ILK and transparent processes to reduce user conflicts, with ecosystem service models for multi-objective planning, especially in data poor high-value sectors, and strategic mapping products for different stakeholders (Lombard et al., 2019). However, the complexity of coordination and costs in the ocean are challenging. For example, seafloor mapping is intensive and expensive, leaving most of the planet unmapped (Rivers et al., 2022). Additionally, while land planning often occurs at local scales, sea planning typically spans national and sometimes transnational scales. Planning has high transformative potential, particularly in changing structures, values and practices, by fostering innovative participatory processes at the local level, and promoting social cohesion through collaborative building of prospective scenarios for a common territory (Guardamagna & Cueto, 2015). The main challenges in implementing these large-scale plans include the complexity of coordinating policy across multilevel governments, insufficient citizen participation and representation of local interests, power imbalances among stakeholders, inadequate institutional capacities and insufficient funding for monitoring and enforcement over time (Flannery et al., 2019). Implementation failures due to these challenges can lead to medium-and long-term loss of biodiversity and transformation of ecosystems (e.g. Hailu et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2019). Conversely, positive impacts on ecological and cultural aspects of territories occur when these processes are carefully evaluated and adjusted (e.g. Gurran et al., 2015; Peskett et al., 2023; Short et al., 2023).

title: Integrated water infrastructure
definition: Integrated water infrastructure includes integrated approaches to the management of water storage infrastructure for multiple uses, including storage in natural ecosystems, built infrastructure and combinations of these, and managing these infrastructures in ways that recognize co-dependencies towards the delivery of a targeted societal service (such as meeting water supply needs) and sustaining ecosystems (GWP, 2021). The response option envisages the management of water resources at a basin level, rather than political divisions (García, 2008; Hezri & Dom, 2017; Nesheim et al., 2010) which is also the intent of the European Union Water Framework Directive (Rimmert et al., 2020) and is applicable globally. Implementing this response option requires water actors to work together with actors in biodiversity (e.g., national park and wetland managers) and climate change (e.g., climate change adaptation planners) to enable (a) a more strategic focus on water storage; (b) measuring and modelling storage in an integrated way; (c) engaging stakeholders to define the storage needed and the trade-offs; and (d) using an integrated planning methodology to identify and prioritize investments in natural and built water storage (Boelee et al., 2017; Oral et al., 2020). Integrated water infrastructure has well-established benefits for water for both humans and ecosystems. Providing water for food is also one of the core outcomes of this response option, for example, in enhancing water use efficiency for food security (Bindra et al., 2014; Ward et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2016; Zarghaami, 2006) and reducing risks of water-related disasters (Debele et al., 2023). Conceptualizations such as green and blue water flows (Falkenmark & Rockström, 2006) and the water footprint (Hoekstra, 2017; Hoekstra & Mekonnen, 2012) have deepened the water for food discourse by bringing in a holistic understanding of the impact of food on water resources. The ecosystem approach can enable better consideration of biodiversity (such as the role of native wetland vegetation in buffering water regimes in certain situations), building upon the co-production of knowledge and modelling (Hülsmann et al., 2019) which draws from multiple sources, including ILK (such as incorporating ecological and evolutionary understanding in ecosystem management) (Jessen et al., 2022; Vollmer et al., 2022). Evidence of the influence of this response option on health is inconclusive but some benefits have been shown on water, sanitation and hygiene, water for ecosystems and other dimensions (Volenzo & Odiyo, 2018) (Bunch et al., 2011). Pathways connecting the response option to climate change mitigation are linked with the coupling of water and carbon cycles and the role of water management in sustaining carbon stores (Santoni et al., 2021; Stachowicz et al., 2022). While this response option can benefit food production and ecological function, it has high economic costs. The integrated approach supports a wide range of SDGs beyond water (SDG6), including those related to health (SDG3), agriculture (SDG2), poverty (SDG1), energy (SDG7), climate change (SDG13), biodiversity (SDGs 14 and 15), gender (SDG5) and peace (SDG16) (UNEP, 2021). An example of the use of integrated storage approaches is that of the City of Windhoek, Namibia, which increased storage (the three-dam system) by managing surface and groundwater jointly, investing in direct potable reuse, implementing water demand management and conservation measures, and also used the Windhoek Aquifer as a “water bank” (Delgado et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2019).

title: Transboundary water cooperation
definition: Working across political boundaries to balance water needs across countries and sectors can have global significance with 153 countries having territory within at least one of the 286 transboundary river and lake basins and 592 transboundary aquifer systems (UN & UNESCO, 2021). Transboundary cooperation is mainly supported by cooperative water agreements, which cut across several sectors, including water resources, irrigation, hydropower, environment, biodiversity, agriculture, fisheries and others. For example, the Convention on the Protection and Use of Transboundary Watercourses and International Lakes (Water Convention), adopted in Helsinki in 1992, is an international environmental agreement wherein the parties take actions to prevent, control and reduce transboundary impacts on biodiversity and other nexus elements, use transboundary waters reasonably and equitably and ensure their sustainable management (UNECE, 2018). Successful transboundary cooperation can be enabled by a functional water cooperation mechanism that regulates transboundary water management and diversifies transboundary water governance responsibilities, sharing benefits within and outside transboundary river basins and making systemic efforts to pursue transboundary water management in a sustainable, equitable and integrative manner (Grünwald et al., 2020). Cooperation on transboundary waters cuts across several nexus elements. Examples include cooperation between several Balkan countries which share the Dinaric Karst Aquifer System, which has enabled national and regional management approaches for ecosystem protection (UN & UNESCO, 2021). The Permanent Okavango Basin River Commission’s livelihood and socioeconomic development thematic programme has enabled cooperation between Angola, Botswana and Namibia, and demonstrates ways in which basin-wide strategic development programmes can address underlying drivers of poverty (Permanent Okavango Basin River Water Commission, 2019). The 2012 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement has provided a framework for common action by Canada and the United States of America to reduce “chemicals of mutual concern” that threaten human health and the environment (Government of Canada, 2012). Countries of the lower Mekong River basin have adopted the Mekong Climate Change Adaptation Strategy and Action Plan (Mekong River Commission, 2018) to coordinate climate action. Transboundary cooperation on adaptation and mitigation of climate change can also bring additional benefits, such as conflict prevention, socioeconomic development and human well-being (UN & UNESCO, 2021). title: Groundwater governance
definition: Groundwater, which accounts for approximately 99 per cent of all liquid freshwater on Earth (UN Water, 2022), is threatened by high rates of groundwater storage depletion in several parts of the globe (Bierkens & Wada, 2019), as well as pollution and salinization in coastal areas (Lapworth et al., 2022). However, 2.6 billion people live in river basins where groundwater is needed due to the lack of surface water (Stewart-Koster et al., 2023). Effective groundwater management increases welfare; however, several factors, e.g., economic, hydrologic and agronomic, may lead to situations where the benefits are negligible (Edwards, 2016; Knapp & Olson, 1995; Koundouri, 2004). New forms of decentralized governance specific to groundwater are emerging in response to severe groundwater deficit in various parts of the world, aided by the advent of deep tubewell groundwater lifting technology, state-led incentives for its adoption and de facto groundwater regulatory regimes (Birkenholtz, 2015). It is well established that groundwater governance is best conceptualized as a process and not as a set of descriptive managerial policies. This encompasses the biophysical conditions of the resource and interactions between groundwater users and the resource, and between those between users, communities and the state (Closas & Villholth, 2020). Integral elements of groundwater governance include: updating knowledge on groundwater resources (including cases where these resources are present as ‘fossil-water’) (De Jong et al., 2020; Jasechko et al., 2017); policy and planning at aquifer level while also setting national groundwater visions; management to regulate removing groundwater from aquifers as well as to address the effects on ecosystems, surface waters, land subsidence and other effects; and ensuring availability of tailored finances (UN Water, 2022). Recognition of the significance of institutions, improved availability and access to groundwater information and science, robustness of civil society, and supportive economic and regulatory frameworks are key enablers of effective groundwater governance (Varady et al., 2016). For example, in India, participatory forms of groundwater management based on ‘aquifer-based, common pool resource’ approaches are being used to address rapid declines in groundwater resources in several parts of the country (Kulkarni et al., 2015). Groundwater management can also deliver potential climate change mitigation benefits without detrimental effects to biodiversity and food, however, the role of governance in such projects is yet to be systematically investigated. The potential of saline aquifer formations, onshore and offshore, to store carbon dioxide has been explored (Bachu, 2015; Bachu et al., 2007; Bradshaw et al., 2007; Goodman et al., 2016), however, the energy footprints of such measures have not been considered in such estimates. Projects in the North Sea and Canada have demonstrated the potential of large geological storage of carbon dioxide in saline aquifers (i.e., 1 Mt of CO2 per year) (Government of Alberta, 2019). Adaptation to climate change-induced water stress is increasingly employing groundwater-based adaptations, such as managed aquifer recharge (Dillon et al., 2020). Groundwater is linked to at least 53 targets in SDGs 6, 12, 13 and 15 of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (UN Water, 2022) While in most of the cases there exists reinforcing linkages between achieving the target and trends or aspirations regarding groundwater, conflicts also exist for a few such as SDG Target 7.1 (access to reliable and affordable energy), which may negatively affect groundwater quality (Guppy et al., 2018).

title: Water-sensitive urban infrastructure
definition: This response option focuses on applying principles of Water Sensitive Urban Design in the design of urban infrastructure to conserve water while simultaneously protecting the health and biodiversity of waterways and mitigating the risk of damage to life and property from flooding (Rashetnia et al., 2022). Water Sensitive Urban Design systems are applicable globally in all urban areas, being of greatest value in those that are prone to water-related risks (Ahammed, 2017; Radcliffe et al., 2017). They are implemented at a range of scales from the household to city levels. Water Sensitive Urban Design systems can encapsulate a range of interventions from building infrastructure for the drainage and harvesting of stormwater to the installation of treatment facilities for the removal of water-borne pollutants (A. K. Sharma et al., 2016). They can also be implemented to improve urban landscapes by incorporating built reservoirs/ wetlands into the planning process (de Graaf & van der Brugge, 2010; Rashetnia et al., 2022). Water Sensitive Urban Design systems that implement infrastructure for the collection and storage of stormwater improve the availability of water for human use (Fewkes, 2012; Rashetnia et al., 2022). Water Sensitive Urban Design systems can also enhance biodiversity and the ecological functioning of urban environments and natural lands (Findlay & Taylor, 2006; Ranta et al., 2021), and can make urban-adjacent environments more ecologically resilient (Ranta et al., 2021). As one of the primary objectives of Water Sensitive Urban Design systems is to mitigate urban flooding risk, they can benefit the health and well-being of urban residents

title: Community water management
definition: Community water management is based on the premise that water challenges at the local level can be overcome if communities collectively develop their own behavioural choices and build social capital regarding the beneficial effects of collective action (Syabri et al., 2014). Placing communities at the heart of water management solutions, community water management recognizes the potential for local solutions to emerge from human networks, social interactions and local knowledge (Dean et al., 2016), which also result in benefits for biodiversity. Collective action to manage water commons may also include setting contextualized incentive-based rules, thus providing flexibility in contrast with a common and control-based approach setting specific parameters such as irrigation technology mandates (Allen & Smith, 2023). These actions, especially in rural settings, are relevant globally but implemented locally (Abeywardana et al., 2018; Krishan, 2011; Ostrom, 1990; Rodriguez De San Miguel et al., 2015). Nexus approaches can support community water management in various ways. For example, modern small-scale decentralized hydro-power based energy solutions in select low income countries have the potential for co-benefits in food security, income, health, the empowerment of women and resource conservation when synergies between these solutions and elements of the nexus are considered in programme development and implementation (Guta et al., 2017). Nexus approaches have also been used to provide insights into the linkages between sustainable energy projects and the food and water sectors to avoid trade-offs and enhance development outcomes and impacts of energy projects (Karan et al., 2018; Perrone et al., 2011; Terrapon-Pfaff et al., 2018). Since the 1970s, water user associations have emerged to improve coverage and efficiency in low-performing state-managed irrigation systems as well as to improve small-scale community-based and farmer-led irrigation systems (Mollinga et al., 2007; Playán et al., 2018), and rural drinking water (Bisung et al., 2014; Hasan et al., 2020; Madrigal-Ballestero et al., 2013) with varying success. Through visioning and prioritization, knowledge-sharing and story-telling, the capacity of communities to act as valued environmental stewards increased (Reeves & Bonney, 2023). Similarly, collective action can be targeted at adaptation to water scarcity, including those triggered by climate change (Murtinho, 2016), yet demonstration of the effectiveness is limited. Community-based water stewardship around locally-led adaptation, when supported with inclusion, diverse and democratized knowledge and equity and justice could provide an important opportunity for greater climate-resilient development (Rahman et al., 2022). Community-led initiatives are considered technically feasible and socially acceptable. They already contribute at a local scale to several SDGs, and even to synergies between different goals (Henfrey et al., 2023). In several cases, these initiatives have pre-empted many aspirations of the 2030 Agenda to integrate diverse environmental and social goals (Henfrey, 2018).

title: City region food systems
definition: City region food systems address sustainability of urban food systems through integrated strategies (Vieira et al., 2018) that include social values (liveability), health (diets, pollution, mobility) and total environmental footprint (X. Bai et al., 2022). The city region focus provides the capacity to integrate impacts across supply chains, account for localized externalities and leverage proximate environmental and commercial relationships with adjacent rural communities. City region food systems borrow from the concepts of integrated landscape approaches with the distinction that municipal governance provides an integrated policymaking space that is frequently missing in integrated landscape approaches (Estrada-Carmona et al., 2014). City governance, with its focus on enhancing liveability, demonstrates a heightened sensitivity to human well-being compared to governance at other scales (Oliveira et al., 2015). Moreover, this scale is better suited to tackle complex challenges, such as the need for integrated governance, territorial development and the ramifications of food, water, and environmental changes on human health (Ayambire et al., 2019; X. Bai et al., 2016; Blay-Palmer et al., 2018). City region food systems emphasize both green spaces within city limits and in the proximate peri-urban spaces, largely rural, as uniquely adapted to providing nature-based solutions in spaces with dense human occupation. Such nature-based solutions, implemented by rural farming communities, include, but are not limited to, improving air quality, food production, disaster risk mitigation, recreational space contributing to mental health, and regulating water quality and quantity (Lafortezza et al., 2018). Proximity to peri-urban systems enables closed-loop material flows (Boudet et al., 2020) and fosters socioeconomic connections between rural producers and urban consumers, reducing the anonymity and marginalization of farmer communities (Daghagh Yazd et al., 2019; Gregoire, 2002). It enhances farmer responsibility for reducing degradation pressures and elevates recognition for their contributions to sustainability (Fremier et al., 2013; Lecegui et al., 2023). For example, pollution from food production affects dense urban populations directly (Bell et al., 2011; Schaider et al., 2019), incurring mitigation costs such as water treatment and health costs associated with respiratory ailments (Bray et al., 2019; Mittal et al., 2009). City region food systems have strong demands on, and incentives to improve, the management of water. A growing number of cities are recognizing and actively managing peri-urban agriculture to mitigate flood risks (Gunnell et al., 2019; Quagliolo et al., 2021) and to improve water quality while reducing treatment costs. Cities concentrate food waste (Fattibene et al., 2020) with unique economic opportunities to reduce and transform waste, including waste water, to resource compost (Pai et al., 2019; Rashid & Shahzad, 2021), feed (Cheng & Lo, 2016; Fowles & Nansen, 2020) or energy (Curry & Pillay, 2012; Wong, 2022). Full recovery of wastewater could recover and reuse 13.4 per cent of global demand for nutrients while decreasing pollution (Mateo-Sagasta et al., 2015; Qadir et al., 2020) though is increasingly challenged by chemical pollution of sewage sludge originating from urban sources (Delibacak et al., 2020; Mateo-Sagasta et al., 2015). Making urban and peri-urban land available for food production (Perrin & Baysse-Lainé, 2020) generates localized employment and connects rural and urban citizens (Firth et al., 2011). title: Integrated watershed-health interventions
definition: Health interventions have been developed explicitly within integrated landscape and watershed management (Basuki et al., 2022; Jupiter et al., 2013; Thapa et al., 2022), integrated landscape-seascape approaches and ecosystem health (‘Ecohealth’) approaches (Horwitz & Finlayson, 2011; A. Jenkins et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2012). These vary in focus, scale and the degree of integration with health departments or within broader health promotion (Nishi & Hashimoto, 2022). They are specific, place-based responses, as illustrated in Box featuring a successful and well documented example from Watershed Interventions for Systems Health in Fiji (WISH Fiji) (Jupiter et al., 2023). Protected catchments provide clean water for people and the environment, including coastal fisheries. Such catchments reduce the distribution and transmission of waterborne diseases, such as leptospirosis, typhoid and dengue which have increased incidence associated with flooding and extreme weather events (Nelson et al., 2022). Under-5 mortality involving diarrhoea particularly occurs in rural areas where most drinking water is sourced direct from (microbially polluted) local catchments (Prüss-Ustün, Wolf, et al., 2019). Restoration of vegetation to protect catchments has further benefits: enhanced carbon sequestration and the reduction of landslides, flooding and the impact of extreme weather events (Stosch et al., 2017). In addition, reducing nutrient and sediment pollution of coastal water protects marine health. Such pollution is a top-ranked pressure on coral reefs worldwide (Andrello et al., 2022). title: Urban nature-based solutions*
definition: Urban nature-based solutions are a common response option to address multiple sustainable development goals in urbanized populated areas (Babí Almenar et al., 2021; Carvalho et al., 2022; Goodwin et al., 2023; Kabisch et al., 2016, 2022; Kalantari et al., 2023; Raymond et al., 2017). Urban nature-based solutions range from urban forests to sustainable urban drainage systems (Escobedo et al., 2019; European Commission. Directorate General for Research and Innovation., 2021; Ruangpan et al., 2020), and are regarded as an “umbrella concept of established urban ecosystem-based approaches” (Kabisch et al., 2022, p. 1388; also: Babí Almenar et al., 2021; Bayulken et al., 2021; Frantzeskaki et al., 2019; Goodwin et al., 2023). However, implementation remains geographically concentrated in the Global North (Grace et al., 2021; Moosavi et al., 2021). Differences in infrastructure, attitudes towards public spaces and more decentralized governance in the Global South may limit the utility of conclusions from the academic literature (Diep et al., 2022; Goodwin et al., 2023; Kabisch et al., 2022; Keeler et al., 2019; Nassary et al., 2022; Wolff et al., 2022). This is even more salient considering a key factor for urban nature-based solutions implementation is attention to context (Kabisch et al., 2022; B. B. Lin et al., 2021).
