title: Dam operation
definition: Allowing water releases from dams that mimic a natural flow regime is well established to maintain or increase biodiversity, connectivity of floodplains, and ecological resilience (Arthington et al., 2023; Poff & Zimmerman, 2010; Tickner et al., 2020; Tockner et al., 2000), but ecological responses are often context and scale-dependent. Dam removal, which is growing in social acceptability, to help restore natural flows (Stanley & Doyle, 2003) is an increasingly popular management action to help maintain or restore native biodiversity. However, flows can also balance biodiversity needs with other uses (Chen & Olden, 2017). Dam water releases can affect a larger geographic scale when dams are operated together (Opperman et al., 2019) and can balance multiple needs that link environmental flows with migration, trade, tourism and disease spread (IPBES, 2019). Dam operations directly affect the delivery of water quantity and quality for both people and ecosystems. However, multiple demands on water resources, such as hydropower, irrigation, drinking water and biodiversity, are often conflicting. For example, implementing environmental flows from dams could reduce the potential for irrigated agriculture to contribute to global food production by reducing water withdrawals and irrigated areas (Bonsch et al., 2015). However, flow releases can improve fisheries and livelihoods and human well-being (Adams et al., 2023; A. Harwood, 2017). Dam operations may also accommodate traditional fishing and cultivation practices without substantial trade-offs on food security and hydropower (Chen & Olden, 2017; Sabo et al., 2017). Dam water releases can have negative impacts on human health through increased access and proximity to water which can increase vector-borne and other diseases and pollute drinking water for downstream villages (Lund et al., 2022; Ramamurthy et al., 2023). However, modifying dam releases may help with malaria control with minimal trade-offs for other uses (Lund et al., 2022). Adjusting dam releases shows potential economic benefits from electricity and agricultural production, and flood damage control (Amjath-Babu et al., 2019). Environmental flows have societal support, align with political priorities and are incorporated into water basin management plans or assessment strategies (Tickner et al., 2020). They can consider different social and cultural views, but financial values such as hydropower and fisheries harvests are given higher value (Capon & Capon, 2017) and could lead to inequities in the implementation of flows. Moreover, dam operations such as the decision to hold or release water downstream can provide water for food production, healthy lives and sanitation, but holding water released downstream may also increase the burden of disease (Lund et al., 2022). Economic assessments of environmental flow policies show the potential effectiveness of water trading as the value of instream flows for environmental reasons was similar to or greater than agricultural uses, however, successful approaches require a basin-wide viewpoint and multi-stakeholder dialogues (Colby, 2020; Grafton, 2019).

title: Ecosystem-based adaptation in rural landscapes
definition: Ecosystem-based adaptation is increasingly incorporated into national and international biodiversity and climate policies to address climate change challenges and achieve the SDGs (IUCN, 2020b; Pörtner et al., 2021; N. Seddon, 2022; United Nations Environment Programme, 2022b, 2022a). Ecosystem-based climate change adaptation uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to reduce people’s vulnerability to climate change by facilitating adaption and building resilience to its adverse effects (Chausson et al., 2020; Cohen-Shacham et al., 2016; Colloff et al., 2020; Lavorel et al., 2015; Woroniecki et al., 2023). In rural landscapes the conservation, management and restoration of natural or biodiversity rich semi-natural ecosystems for climate change adaptation delivers multiple benefits to biodiversity and other nexus elements (Key et al., 2022). The management and restoration of forests, wetlands and coastal vegetation provides ecological disaster risk regulation, improves water quality, secures resilient food production, wood for energy and construction and can mitigate climate change. In some cases of forest restoration, it can however reduce food and water quantity (Cohen-Shacham et al., 2016; Pörtner et al., 2021; WWF, 2021). The conservation, restoration and extensive, often traditional, management of high biodiversity, semi-natural grasslands supports adaptation by delivering climate-resilient livestock production, wild foods and medicines, sequestering soil carbon and contributing multiple social and cultural benefits (Bardgett et al., 2021; Lavorel et al., 2015). While implementation of ecosystem-based adaptation is often led by local public institutions (e.g., municipalities or local governments), multiple models of governance often coexist within individual regions. These have varying levels of co-design and participation, and inclusion of multiple knowledge systems and world views, especially ILK so that Indigenous and traditional values and knowledge are represented (Dubo et al., 2023; Pascual et al., 2022). In Japan, wetland restoration for geese populations and flood risk management was led by a conservation NGO with government support, which has now scaled out to multiple sites across the region by proving benefits to farmers initially reticent regarding yield loss (Cohen-Shacham et al., 2016). In Germany, governance of nature-based flood management and mitigation spans four governance models: top-down government, government-led co-design, public and citizen cooperation and initiatives, and citizen-led governance (Zingraff-Hamed et al., 2021). Although fewer reported cases involve rights-based instruments and customary norms or social and cultural options, consideration of multiple values and world views alongside knowledge systems (including ILK) are essential to nature-based transformative adaptation of rural landscapes (Colloff et al., 2020; Fedele et al., 2020). Transformative adaptation is defined as systemic changes to societal paradigms, visions, goals, rules and knowledge in response to actual or anticipated changes in driver variables that fundamentally change the properties of a social-ecological system (IPBES, 2019b). Three critical mechanisms for nature-based adaptation and transformation in rural landscapes directly relate to empowerment and multi-stakeholder co-production: (i) traditional management of multifunctionality, especially at the landscape level; (ii) collective management and governance; and (iii) construction of values and uses for nature’s contributions to adaptation (Donatti et al., 2020; N. A. Kirk & Cradock-Henry, 2022; Lavorel et al., 2020; Werners et al., 2021). Scaling ecosystem-based adaptation is a pressing challenge, requiring the amplification of local successful projects to multiple locations (scaling out) and scaling up to required changes in knowledge, governance and their interactions (Colloff et al., 2021; Dubo et al., 2023; United Nations Environment Programme, 2022b).

title: Net-zero sustainable healthcare
definition: Healthcare providers and the health sector broadly are addressing the need for urgent action to safeguard health by reducing their carbon and environmental footprints. This is being done by changing practices (including increased prevention and community care to reduce the need for hospitalisation), and materials, energy sources and procurement across supply chains (Andrieu et al., 2023). Over sixty countries pledged action to achieve net-zero sustainable healthcare following the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change COP26 Health Programme and more than 68,000 hospitals and health centres in 81 countries are members of Healthcare Without Harm’s Global Green and Healthy Hospitals network (Romanello et al., 2021; Wise, 2021). The impact of transforming healthcare can be estimated as a reduction of 2.26 × 10-4 excess deaths from heat, per ton of greenhouse gas emissions avoided per year (Bressler, 2021). Healthcare carbon footprints range from 1.51 t/greenhouse gas/per capita in resource-intensive healthcare in the United States of America to 0.06 t/greenhouse gas/per capita in

title: Urban green infrastructure
definition: Urban green infrastructure broadly defined as a network of natural, semi-natural and artificial green spaces that deliver multiple ecosystem services (European Commission, 2013), is a strategy to transform urban environments to be more healthy, liveable and biodiverse (WHO, 2016). Management of urban green and blue spaces affects the health and well-being of over 50 per cent of the global population (UN, 2019). However, only 27 per cent global urban centres had adequate greenspace in 2021 (Romanello et al., 2022). This response option complements others with a focus on urban and peri-urban forests and trees, which can be a cost-effective way to improve health outcomes and address multiple socioecological needs. Urban green infrastructure provides multiple health benefits (Superior Health Council, 2021). Green space metrics are associated with reduced cardiovascular, respiratory and heat-related mortality (Gascon et al., 2016; K. L. Wolf et al., 2020) and increased life expectancy (R. Connolly et al., 2023; Idrovo, 2011). Urban green infrastructure is consistently associated with better mental health, elevated mood levels and lower anxiety across life stages (K. O. Lee et al., 2023; K. L. Wolf et al., 2020). Increasing tree canopy could potentially reduce hundreds of premature deaths within a single urban area, valued at billions of dollars (Kondo, Mueller, et al., 2020). Urban trees can increase biodiversity and ecosystem resilience (Morgenroth & Armstrong, 2012). High tree diversity areas support more animal diversity and are more resilient to climate change, pests and diseases than tree monocultures (Cowett & Bassuk, 2020). Publicly accessible fruit and nut trees also improve food access and reduce food insecurity (K. H. Clark & Nicholas, 2013). Urban green infrastructure also filters stormwater pollutants and helps maintain local water supplies (Kuehler et al., 2016), further benefitting health. Moreover, it can improve ecological connectivity (Munshi-South, 2012; Von Thaden et al., 2021), but knowledge gaps remain around which configurations maximize connectivity regionally (LaPoint et al., 2015) and how to minimize vector-borne disease risks (Heylen et al., 2019). title: Biodiversity management for zoonoses
definition: Zoonotic diseases include those of pandemic potential such as COVID-19, with estimates from the WHO of approximately 0.8 billion cases worldwide by late-June 2021). However, global funding and scientific research is lower for zoonotic neglected tropical diseases despite their impacts on disability-adjusted life years (Goarant et al., 2019; McIntyre et al., 2017). Stopping biodiversity loss has been presented as the best prevention strategy to limit the risk of spillover at source and spread of emerging zoonotic diseases (IPBES, 2020; Roche et al., 2020), while reducing the costs of response to pandemics (Bernstein et al., 2022). However, the relationship with biodiversity is multidirectional and often highly disease-specific such that increased conservation by itself is not assured to prevent zoonotic diseases emergence (Morand, 2020). It is also dependent on context – countries with effective surveillance, coordinated health systems ), and trust in government have experienced better responses to outbreaks (One Health High-Level Expert Panel (OHHLEP) et al., 2023). Interactions across nexus elements have critical roles in this response option (Malecela & Ducker, 2021) but have not been fully assessed. Climate change is an important driver for zoonotic diseases spread (McIntyre et al., 2017; Romanello et al., 2022), and more than half of zoonotic infectious diseases can be aggravated by climate change (Mora et al., 2022). Climate change is also increasing direct threats on biodiversity including the wildlife hosts and vectors of diseases (Pörtner et al., 2021), stressing the interlinkages between health, biodiversity and climate (Atwoli et al., 2021; Malecela & Ducker, 2021). Globally, water resources are under stress, increasing water insecurity and threatening freshwater biodiversity (Grill et al., 2019; Vörösmarty et al., 2010). The increasing number of dams (Mulligan et al., 2020) favours emerging water-and vector-borne diseases (Kibret et al., 2021; McFarlane et al., 2013; Sleigh et al., 2006; Ziegler et al., 2013). The protection of wetlands, which were historically linked with unsanitary living conditions, is seen as a key approach to reduce the spread of emerging infectious diseases such as avian flu (Wu et al., 2020). Agricultural expansion has major negative impacts on biodiversity, climate change, pollution and invasive species (Crist et al., 2017; Zabel et al., 2019). Significant relationships between zoonotic disease outbreaks with expanding human demography, livestock, poultry, tree plantation and artificial land expansion suggest that changes to the global food system could reduce the risk of emerging infectious diseases (Morand, 2022) and contribute to many of the SDGs (M. Clark et al., 2022; Lajaunie & Morand, 2021). The consumption of wildlife and wildlife farming are further zoonotic risks (IPBES, 2020). The definition of the prevention of spillover at source (OHHLEP et al., 2023) identifies factors to be addressed as using a nexus approach and taking into account the socioeconomic context and wildlife supply chain (Kock & Caceres-Escobar, 2022). This has the potential to address equity issues, e.g., for those involved in wildlife procurement or sale, and reduce economic costs through a more complex approach to prevention. This approach stresses that the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (i.e., target 5) (CBD, 2022) should explicitly implement the objective of spillover risk reduction (Caceres-Escobar et al., 2023).

title: Health impact assessments
definition: Health impact assessment is an approach to assess the potential health effects of a policy, programme or project on a population (particularly on vulnerable or disadvantaged groups) that may follow international (WHO, 2023b) or other guidelines (e.g., (e.g., European Centre for Health Policy, 1999)). Stakeholder and community engagement, equity, ethical use of evidence, sustainable development and use across sectors are core features (WHO, 2023b). Health impact assessments help decision-makers make choices about alternatives and improvements to prevent disease or injury and to actively promote health. The approach recognizes the small extent to which health is considered within environmental impact assessments and emphasizes the importance of the learning process to envision a holistic approach to health and well-being (Cameron et al., 2011). The community health impact assessments are an extension of the health impact assessment; they empower communities to conduct health impact assessments, to use the information and results gained, and to negotiate during public policymaking processes (Leuenberger et al., 2022; Pengkam, 2012). The community health impact assessment is an example of co-production of knowledge between a local community, scientists and policymakers, and a learning process that can lead to changes in unsustainable practices and foster increased understanding of health issues resulting from development projects and policies through collective attempts to find solutions. title: The One Health approach
definition: As a holistic approach, One Health has the potential for mobilizing a transformation of governance, socioeconomic systems, habits and mindsets towards nexus approaches (Pascual et al., 2022). The IPBES Workshop Report on Biodiversity and Pandemics (IPBES, 2020), for example, noted the importance of strengthening One Health approaches to pandemic prevention by addressing issues such as sustainable land use, biodiversity conservation, wildlife trade, deforestation and integrated surveillance systems, in addition to public health measures. Other diseases associated with food production (such as avian influenza, foot and mouth disease, antimicrobial resistance) and ecosystems (such as many neglected tropical diseases, plant diseases and insect pest species in forests and cropland) are also successfully addressed with One Health approaches. Antimicrobial resistance is one of the areas where the One Health approach has perhaps made the most significant progress in terms of operationalization. The spread of resistant microorganisms and resistance determinants across human, animal and environmental compartments, combined with the shortage of new antimicrobial drugs has raised the alarm for the need of integrated and interdisciplinary approaches at both national and international levels. The WHO online catalogue of antimicrobial resistance national action plans is a good testimony of the broad utilization of One Health in fighting this often-called silent pandemic (WHO, 2024). However, assessing the impact and success of One Health initiatives across food, biodiversity, water and climate change domains often presents a challenge given the complexity of policy coordination across different sectors and the frequent anthropocentric focus of many of these policies, the power imbalances among stakeholders, and prevailing lack of funding for preventive approaches (Coghlan et al., 2021). Studies have shown that prevention costs guided by a One Health approach would range between $10.3 billion to $11.5 billion annually, compared to the cost of managing pandemics which, according to the recent estimate by the G20 Joint Finance and Health Taskforce, amounts to about $30.1 billion per year (Dobson et al., 2020; Falzon et al., 2018; World Bank, 2022). One Health can strengthen the protection and promotion of healthy ecosystems and the technical feasibility of such initiatives has been established but they require adaptation to local contexts and issues. title: Multi-hazard early warning systems
definition: The Sixth IPCC Assessment Report underscores the direct effects of climate change on extreme events and associated hazards that threaten both human health and ecosystems, particularly the most vulnerable populations living in fragile environments (IAP, 2023; IPCC, 2021). Multi-hazard early warning systems are designed to anticipate, predict and generate warnings for individual or multiple hazards, allowing communities and administrations to prepare, respond and recover effectively and thus build resilience against socio-economic and environmental changes (Fakhruddin et al., 2021; ILO, 2017; UNDRR, 2007; UNISDR, 2015). However, the one-way flow of information is limiting in addressing multi-dimensional risk communication that influences local response attributed to various factors such as trust, knowledge, heuristics, experience or socio-cultural contexts (Khan et al., 2017). Integrated risk communication with multi-hazards early warning systems thus ensures that communities receive, understand and act on impending hazard alerts and that they are adapted to local circumstances and needs (ILO, 2022). By providing timely warnings for multiple hazards across the globe, such as thunderstorms, flooding, cyclones, heatwaves, water scarcity, food security, earthquakes and diseases, multi-hazard early warning systems and risk communication aid both key stakeholders and communities and thus impact the nexus elements (N. Liu et al., 2022; R. Newell, 2023; Prabhakar, 2012; WMO, 2023). Multi-hazard early warning systems collect and process data then communicate and coordinate through assigned authorities of a jurisdiction. This process necessitates collaborative actions from related stakeholders. For example, in healthcare, multi-hazard early warning systems monitor heat, water-borne and vector-borne diseases in changing ecological scenarios that affect agriculture, health and cities (AASSA, 2021; EASAC, 2019; IAP, 2023; NASAC et al., 2022; WHO, 2018). However, the adoption of warning systems varies across regions and hazards, with only half of global countries accessing early warnings. Regions such as Africa and small island developing states especially need support (NASAC et al., 2022; UNDRR & WMO, 2022). A recent initiative from the United Nations aims for “early warning for all” by 2027, highlighting the commitment to regional and social equality (UNDRR, 2022). Multi-hazards early warning systems are also integral to the Sendai Framework of Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) (UNISDR, 2015). The incorporation of ILK with multi-hazards early warning systems and risk communication could further increase their effectiveness through enhanced participation of IPLC (Fakhruddin et al., 2021; ILO, 2017; UNISDR, 2015). The ongoing efforts to mainstream traditional knowledge of risk communication are irregular and tend to vary across countries and regions (Commonwealth of Australia, 2021; Ministry for the Environment, 2022; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change., 2022; NACCC, 2007; NAPCC, 2008).

title: Rights-based approaches
definition: Rights-based approaches to conservation encompass the application of human rights principles to the ownership, governance, access and management of natural resources and biodiversity (Witter & Satterfield, 2019). They also include the rights of nature, the rights of Mother Earth and rights of other non-human entities (Kenrick et al., 2023). This ensures that conservation-related laws/policies, plans and processes do not violate rights and promote human and natural rights as much as possible (HRBWG, 2022). Rights-based approaches can help address the multiple links between conservation and rights, recognizing that exclusionary approaches to conservation can violate rights; that rights are key to supporting conservation contributions of IPLC, women and other rights-holders; and that all people have rights to a healthy, sustainable environment (D. Boyd & Keene, 2021). Rights-based approaches refer to both collective and individual (HRBWG, 2022; H. D. Jonas et al., 2014) procedural rights, such as participation, access to information and Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC; McDermott et al., 2013; Raftopoulos & Short, 2019), as well as substantive rights, e.g., water, land, territory, food and cultural rights (C. Corson et al., 2020; Witter & Satterfield, 2014). A number of concepts and mechanisms exist to support the implementation of rights-based approaches in conservation, such as co-management (N. Dawson et al., 2023); recognition and strengthening of customary and collective rights (Aswani, 2005; Memon & Kirk, 2012); the interdependence of biological and cultural diversity (Gavin et al., 2018; Sterling et al., 2017); ‘decolonization’ approaches (Domínguez & Luoma, 2020); and legal demarcation, titling and reparations for territories (Claridge & Kobei, 2023; Rist et al., 2019). Rights-based approaches generally go beyond inclusive and participatory conservation efforts; they are firmly grounded in recognizing rights. This includes, in particular, the leadership and rights of IPLC in decision-making, management, benefit-sharing and ownership of

title: Inclusive water education
definition: Formal and informal environmental education is a preventive policy and management instrument which contributes to promoting behaviours and recognizing cosmovision and values related to water protection using a holistic approach, 2015/annexes/h2020-wp1415-annex-g-trl_en.pdf. including spiritual and traditional approaches and customary governance systems (Sarkar, 2022). This can also include consideration of biodiversity. Water education, with a gender perspective and including traditional knowledge of IPLC in schools (e.g., using water use and footprint calculations), is a significant first step towards building water consciousness (Sultana, 2018) and effecting behaviour change (Afzal et al., 2022; Koop et al., 2019). In cases where this is not yet achieved, it is important to progress the generation of knowledge so that communities feel challenged and motivated to assume autonomy, responsibility and choice, which enables a transformation of water culture (Lara & Otano, 2017). It is difficult to measure the impact of environmental water education in connection with the nexus elements, except for health. Some studies revealed that higher water knowledge was associated with higher education levels, confirming its importance and allowing identification of potential subgroups that may benefit from targeted support of water management initiatives (Dean et al., 2016). The recognition of the need for education programs is widespread in the different global policy frameworks, e.g., explicitly mentioned in Targets 16 and 21 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework), SDG6 (clean water and sanitation), SDG4 and SDG5 (gender equality) to have a holistic education (COP15, n.d.; Rad et al., 2022). Such awareness-raising activities are important parts of environmental education, for example, to increase knowledge and values promoting the protection and conservation of the environment, e.g., by protecting water sources from contamination and more generally to inform and empower people to help protect water (Woldetsadik et al., 2018).

title: Inclusive water management
definition: Inclusive water management recognizes that there needs to be an inclusive process for participation in water management that includes other cultures, multiple genders and diverse world views (Anderson et al., 2013). This need is also recognized by different international instruments such as the SDGs, Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and Paris Agreement. Others focus on achieving a fairer approach, such as the 1992 Dublin Declaration on Water and Sustainable Development, which recognizes expressly in its principle No. 3 that “Women play a fundamental role in the supply, management and protection of water (United Nations, 2023).” More recently SDG6 established that society must strive to “guarantee the availability of water and its sustainable management and sanitation for all”, with its goals making special mention of the case of women and girls in access to this basic right. The scale of this need ranges from local to national but has applicability wherever inequitable processes occur. Because of gendered roles, responsibilities and asymmetrical power relations in the household and community, interventions that alter access to water can differentially affect women (Bartlett, 1990). The technical feasibility of this response option is high and existing policies are in place to implement it. However, governance involves working within existing institutional structures to create more civic space for women to engage in decision-making that affects their interests (MacArthur et al., 2023). This can lead to the creation of gender-transformative governance programs with an enduring effect. To better engage different genders in water management, policies need to be in place specifically to recognize gender and contribute to women’s participation in all levels of decision-making (ICWE (International Conference on Water and the Environment, 1992). Incorporating a gender approach into integrated water management can lead to more equitable decisions and provide better standards of well-being, psychosocial and physical health and human-environment interactions (Packett et al., 2020). The response option thus has a strong potential to create transformative change. Embedding gender relations and interests within institutional structures can lead to gender-transformative governance programs to better ensure that change and the potential for transformation will be enduring (MacArthur et al., 2023; Pouramin et al., 2020).

title: Rights of nature
definition: The “rights of nature” framework is grounded in the recognition that humanity and nature share a fundamental non-anthropocentric relationship based on valuing biodiversity. Ecocentrism affirms the intrinsic value of the ecosystem, and of each one of its constituents, and biocentrism claims the primordial value of life as a value in and of itself (Borràs, 2016; Boyd, 2017; Nash, 1989; Tanasescu, 2022). The rights of nature approach is also an expression of cosmovisions for some IPLC and involves guaranteeing the right of access to water and the recognition of ecosystems as subjects of law (Olaya López, 2022) (Eduardo, 2015) ). This contrasts with the United Nations General Assembly Resolution 64/292 (2010), which recognizes the human right to access to drinking water and requires states to adopt legislative, administrative, budgetary and judicial measures (United Nations, 2010). There are several examples of legalization of rights of nature from Bangladesh, Bolivia, Bhutan, Colombia, Ecuador, India, Mexico, New Zealand, Uganda and the United States of America (Kahui et al., 2023). The first case that was recognized was the Whanganui River, New Zealand (Rodgers, 2017). This river was granted rights of personhood and later these rights were extended to species and land, online Supplementary material 7.2. The Tūhoe people collectively and the New Zealand government agreed to serve as guardians for the protection of Te Urewera (a majorly forested hill country in the country’s North Island). More recently, rights of nature frameworks have been applied to specific ecosystems, such as wetlands (Davies et al., 2021) and rivers (O’Donnell & Talbot-Jones, 2018). However, application challenges remain, for example, addressing concerns related to assigning personhood to nature and challenges related to accountability and jurisdiction (Kahui et al., 2023; O’Donnell & Talbot-Jones, 2018). Implementing this response option has strong benefits for water and potentially positive impacts on biodiversity and human needs by ensuring ecological flows in rivers (O’Donnell & Talbot-Jones, 2018). However, some studies have noted that recognizing rivers as legal entities may also lead to increased competition where rights of rivers conflict with human water use (Kahui et al., 2023; O’Donnell, 2020). title: Address gendered burdens of water collection
definition: Women often experience increased exposure to impacts of environmental changes (Brown et al., 2023). For example, women can be more vulnerable to the impacts of climate change since they are generally responsible for ensuring the survival of families by providing water and food. Natural disasters such as floods can destroy water systems established specifically for communities that depend on untreated water and health resources, which leads to water pollution (Casas Varez, 2017) ). Given that women use different ecosystem services than men, these differences are important to understand in order to implement more sustainable and equitable policies and interventions (Fortnam et al., 2019). Water collection is challenging due to distance, scarcity and lack of protection. Women face increased risks of disease due to direct contact with poor quality water and attacks during their journey to natural resource sources. For example, water tankers in western Rajasthan benefit upper-caste households, but poor and low-caste households remain dependent on drying water sources, particularly women from low-caste households who walk long distances to access water (Sarkar, 2022). These long distances result in detrimental effect on the health of women of all ages, where water-carrying methods impose physical loads with the potential to cause musculoskeletal disorders and related disability (Geere et al., 2010). This response option focuses on technological tools, educational strategies and economic support that can reduce the burden of water collection on women and girls and, as a result, provide more time to study, work and/ or for leisure (Kayser et al., 2019; Pouramin et al., 2020). It benefits water for humans and provides increased access to healthy foods, which improves human well-being. There is substantial evidence showing connections between water availability and accessibility and well-being including psychosocial health, physical health, personal beliefs, social relationships and human-environment interactions (Kangmennaang & Elliott, 2021). Moreover, diseases increase especially in women and girls due to water access inequalities (Packett et al., 2020) (Pouramin et al., 2020). Improvements in rural water supply allows women to transform the time saved from water collection into money (Crow et al., 2012; James et al., 2002). No evidence was found to show an effect of this response option on biodiversity. Technologies for facilitating improved access to water for women and girls to alleviate time burdens and the detrimental impacts on their health and safety from carrying water can change rapidly and hence evidence on their feasibility is inconclusive. There are international instruments that regulate or recognize gender and water access rights, but some of these include the need for more infrastructure technology, such as connecting water to homes and solar-powered pumps to reduce labour for collection.

title: Foster gender transformative approaches
definition: Women play key roles in food systems (FAO, 2020b) ranging from producing, processing, distributing, marketing and consuming (Funge-Smith & Bennett, 2019). Gender-based discrimination and human rights violations are major causes of poverty and food and nutrition insecurity (N. J. Bennett et al., 2021; FAO, 2023c). Gender often interacts with other forms of discrimination, such as socioeconomic class, age, ethnicity and disability, requiring intersectional analyses and policy responses (Motta, 2021). Responses to address this situation include strengthening women’s access to and control of assets, notably land; better inclusion in value chains, including better access to markets and improving labour conditions and legislation (Ros-Tonen et al., 2019) and greater women’s (economic) empowerment (Njuki et al., 2023; Bryan et al., 2023). However, relatively few studies assess the effectiveness of these responses and even fewer address gender equity in urban or aquatic food contexts. Reviews show mixed impacts on nexus elements of increased tenure security for women. Studies in Uganda and Rwanda demonstrate positive impacts on soil conservation, notably among female-headed households (Ali et al., 2014; Deininger & Ali, 2008). Meinzen-Dick et al. (2019) found weaker evidence of impacts on natural resource management, food security, technology adoption or productivity but strong impacts on bargaining power and decision-making on consumption and (human) capital investment. These mixed findings may relate to how tenure is institutionalized and experienced (Winters et al., 2018), highlighting the need to distinguish legal security and contextual or de facto security (Asaaga et al., 2020; Ghebru, 2019). Women face many hidden costs related to market access and integration, which are systematically overlooked by public and private sector actors and institutions (Pouw et al., 2020; Noack & Pouw, 2015). Such costs are multi-dimensional (economic, social and/or political), creating obstacles for marginalized food entrepreneurs to professionalize and upscale their businesses. They influence risk perceptions, time and resource allocation, and business investment decisions. Innovations supporting inclusive business are only effective when applicable to specific problems and contexts, affordable and accessible to all. Better market access and integration does not automatically improve nutrition security. A review of thirteen projects in Africa and Asia, aimed at improving market access and integration, shows that this is due to a focus on cash crop production and prioritizing business investments and other costs such as health care over buying high quality food (Pouw et al., 2020). Economic inclusion programming – including social safety nets, livelihoods, job and financial inclusion programs – strengthens women’s economic opportunities, income, and asset ownership and supports shifts in gender norms, such as increased mobility (Andrews et al., 2021). Cash or in-kind transfers combined with high-quality complementary programming, such as agricultural extension produce significant improvements in agriculture and nutrition outcomes (PIM, 2021). Generally, efforts to improve gender equity often adopt a narrow focus on women, overlooking men or gender relations (Lawless et al., 2021). This risks putting the blame, or burden for change, on women (Hicks et al., 2022; Bank et al., 2020).

title: Indigenous food systems
definition: Indigenous Peoples and local communities’ (IPLC) food systems integrate cultural dimensions to food (FAO, Alliance of Biodiversity International, & CIAT, 2021). These include access to food from ancestral and structural assets, cosmological and web of life values, sovereignty and sustainable production, and integrative health. However, these food systems face challenges related to land tenure problems (Rudel & Hernandez, 2017), gender issues (Olsen, 2017), social justice (Olivé, 2004), horizontal cooperation (Ghate et al., 2011) and the embracing of plural common vision (McGregor, 2016), which are important considerations in addressing trade-offs between the nexus elements. The future of IPLC food systems depends on the formalization of sustainable and sovereign land use and territory aiming at integrative health that encompasses public health actions, promotion of sustainable healthy diets and respect of traditional food diversity and production. Indigenous and local knowledge provides a distinct understanding of the nexus in relation to the interlinkages among IPLC food systems, biodiversity conservation and human habitats (E. M. Gardner et al., 2022; Hill et al., 2020). These systems are diverse and imply multiple perspectives related to ethics, values and world views (P. Cole, 2017). Critical to IPLC food systems are land access and distribution (Mika et al., 2022) and an emphasis on community-based lifestyles (Masitera, 2020). IPLC food systems are highly adept at navigating sustainable futures, including adaptive responses to water scarcity (Stewart-Harawira, 2020) and climate change (Leal Filho et al., 2022). ILK

title: Access to natural resources and land
definition: Secure access to land is fundamental to sustainable food systems and to addressing the challenges caused by habitat and biodiversity loss, land and water degradation, and GHG emissions (Santpoort et al., 2021). Unequal access to natural resources encompasses aspects of social, ethnic and gender inequalities, and reflects power differentials (N. J. Bennett et al., 2023; Meyfroidt et al., 2022). Recognizing the importance of equitable access, the (FAO, 2022b) produced voluntary guidelines on the responsible governance of tenure of land, fisheries and forests, specifically addressing the needs of vulnerable and marginalized groups such as smallholders, IPLC and women. The FAO guidelines emphasize the importance of local contexts, and the various mechanisms and institutions – formal and informal, individual and communal – through which natural resources are accessed (cf. Ostrom (2012); Peluso & Ribot (2020)), which need to be taken into account when designing tenure systems to secure access. Moving beyond titling and formal registration as the main mechanisms for securing access, the guidelines propose a wider range of policies and legislation, as well as advocacy programmes, to strengthen tenure security for vulnerable groups to promote more equitable and secure access to land, fisheries and forests for these groups. title: Universal health coverage
definition: Universal health coverage using a comprehensive primary healthcare approach includes essential health services and reproductive health and family planning (SDG targets 3.7, 5.6), and reorientates spending from expensive treatment-focused care (which is increasingly unsustainable, see H03) to prevention and healthy living conditions (Binagwaho & Ghebreyesus, 2019; WHO, 2023f). Approximately half the global population do not have access to primary healthcare and almost a billion people are vulnerable to out-of-pocket health spending for healthcare that puts them at risk for poverty (WHO and World Bank, 2021). In practice, access to essential health services are prioritized and impacts on nexus elements are related to proximal human needs (e.g., water for human needs, not the environment) or not reported. This has scope to change with wider recognition of the health impacts of climate change and global emergencies (Ghebreyesus, 2020) and the need for climate-resilient health services as a first line of defence (Romanello et al., 2022). Biodiversity or nature is rarely explicitly addressed in discussion of universal health coverage or primary healthcare (Lauwers et al., 2020) but this may change as access to clean, healthy and sustainable environment becomes critical (Andorra et al., 2022). A stronger case for protecting the environment and restoring biodiversity could be made through better identifying, treating and collecting data on environment-linked diseases. However, providing access to healthcare in biodiverse, remote areas can enhance biodiversity. Universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights has potential to address approximately 121 million unintended births p.a. (Bearak et al., 2020). This and achieving optimal child spacing would improve the lives of millions of women and children and address gender-related barriers to healthcare. This also has potential to significantly reduce population growth and pressures on the nexus elements, although the latter is subject to geographical differences in location and the pressure of per-capita consumption (the higher the per capita consumption level, the lower the ecologically sustainable population (Cafaro et al., 2022; P. Dasgupta, 2021; Tamburino & Bravo, 2021). Although estimates of cost-effectiveness of healthcare coverage vary widely due to various methodological, empirical and value driven factors (e.g., Pichon-Riviere et al., 2023), studies indicate that expanding population level and

title: Intercultural health services
definition: Intercultural healthcare is an approach that aims to bridge the gap between Indigenous and Western (or biomedical) health systems, emphasizing mutual recognition and respect of different knowledges, the scope of these medical practices and the conditions that they treat (Torri, 2012). They are formal arrangements between health departments and traditional health practitioners to provide dual health services. Notable examples of biomedical health systems integrated with traditional medicine are found in India (with Ayurvedic practices) and in China (with traditional Chinese medicine) and are also found in New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Brazil, Suriname, Chile and Colombia, among other countries (Patwardhan et al., 2005). Access to intercultural healthcare programs and services could benefit around 476.6 million Indigenous Peoples representing ∼6.2 per cent of the world’s population (Brondízio et al., 2021). It is estimated that approximately 80 per cent of the world's population, both Indigenous Peoples and other traditional and local communities, use traditional healthcare and medicinal plants. However, the best treatment for many diseases includes modern medical and surgical knowledge delivered with respect to cultural and traditional practice (WHO, 2023d). Recognition of cultural determinants of health are essential in reducing differences in health outcomes in IPLC in Australia (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2022) and have been shown to improve community well-being, in Chile, Suriname and Colombia (O’Neill et al., 2007). As demonstrated in Brazil (R. S. Walker et al., 2015), recently contacted Indigenous populations are vulnerable to adverse effects of biomedical care. Intercultural health services have a key role to play in the management of emerging risks, such as food insecurity, water insecurity and vector-borne disease (Hofmeijer et al., 2013). They significantly advance the goal of providing nutritious and culturally appropriate food, a critical component of overall well-being (Anderson et al., 2016; Diamond, 2018; Montenegro & Stephens, 2006; Popkin & Reardon, 2018). Noteworthy initiatives have been undertaken in Thailand, Canada and Colombia (Kuhnlein & Chotiboriboon, 2022; O’Neill et al., 2007). Holistic approaches to health that incorporate respect and care for nature are features of many Indigenous health systems. These are undermined by loss of access by IPLC to their lands and resources and from the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss. The therapeutic properties of treatments are also affected by these factors. As the productivity of agro-ecosystems is reduced, traditional medicines compete poorly with biomedical healthcare (Patwardhan et al., 2023). A potential trade-off of intercultural health services involves the use of wild animal products as traditional medicine or as a health food. Species may be threatened so that biodiversity becomes a trade-off with health. In China, traditional and allopathic medical care systems are closely integrated, and large hospitals commonly use both wild plant and animal products for healthcare. Some of these practices, e.g., the butchering process or drinking raw blood, are potential pathways for zoonotic infection and therefore a trade-off with health itself (Gbogbo & Daniels, 2019; USAID, 2017; Wassenaar & Zou, 2020). Intercultural health services are demonstrating effectiveness in providing cost-effective solutions. Traditional health services, often the first choice for various conditions, result in significant savings for biomedical health services (Ministerio de Salud (Chile), 2021; O’Neill et al., 2007). However, traditional healers often face a lack of professional recognition and receive no monetary compensation for their services, for example, traditional midwives in Bolivia and Guetemala collaborating with hospitals have no expenses covered (M. A. Martin & Gurven, 2022; O’Neill et al., 2007). However, in some places such as remote Australia, Canada and New Zealand healthcare systems support traditional healers (Asamoah et al., 2023; Hawthorne, 2020). Intercultural health services are also key in promoting equity, particularly in access to healthcare as community driven responses including Indigenous knowledge, go beyond conventional healthcare systems, with a strong emphasis on cultural relevance and Indigenous self-governance (O’Neill et al., 2007). Reorienting health services and governance systems based on the capabilities of Indigenous Peoples (Bockstael & Watene, 2016), strengthens control over resources ad land (Peña et al., 2020; Sterling et al., 2017). IPLC’ traditional medical practices link cultural and biological diversity and recognizing these through intercultural health services has potential to be transformative. However, cultural values are undermined when these practices are decontextualized, commoditized or appropriated. Unsustainable demand for traditional medicines can lead to a negative effect on the nexus elements and on the IPLC who are legitimate holders of this knowledge (UNEP, 2023). Traditional medicines may be commercialized and distributed back to communities for profit, devoid of any communal benefits (Rose et al., 2012). Additionally, some rituals and practices, such as the consumption of specific plants or fungi, have gained popularity among outsiders for recreational purposes, inadvertently causing displeasure among spiritual entities and inducing scarcity for IPLC. Biopiracy threatens equitable distribution of benefits derived from ILK and biodiversity used to address Indigenous health issues. Brazil has addressed this by introducing new regulations focusing on access, benefit sharing, utilization or third-party transfer (Sirakaya, 2019).

title: Natural capital accounting
definition: Natural capital accounting is designed as an economic and financial approach to account for the value of natural assets, aiming to shift current economic and market dynamics towards sustainable nature use by identifying, valuing and possibly pricing natural assets. It introduces financial incentives or disincentives for the activities of economic actors, thus addressing interactions between nexus elements in an economy (Kelemen et al., 2022). As an emerging framework at national and regional levels, natural capital accounting seeks to integrate nature’s values into public and business accounts, potentially laying the groundwork for new fiscal systems and biodiversity payments (Dasgupta, 2021; European Commission. Statistical Office of the European Union., 2020; IPBES, 2022a; Kelemen et al., 2022; United Nations Environment Programme, 2022a). Natural capital accounting measures the resources consumed by economic entities and their impacts on ecosystem services in either or both physical and monetary terms. This measurement aims to incorporate benefits of nature historically excluded from markets and treated as externalities, thereby informing economic decision-making (Bagstad et al., 2021; United Nations et al., 2017). However, integrating natural capital accounting into actionable steps presents challenges, including the balance between the system's complexity and its usability for decision-makers. Often, national policies simplify these accounts to biophysical measures, e.g., areas or tons, and thus neglect sociocultural values (United Nations Statistics Division, 2023). Natural capital accounting enriches traditional accounting frameworks by incorporating natural capital data, enabling the analysis of trade-offs among natural, built and human capital within standard economic indicators such as gross domestic product for informed decision-making (La Notte & Rhodes, 2020; Vallecillo et al., 2019). The System of Environmental Economic Accounting framework, developed by the United Nations, represents the most advanced natural capital information system, expanding national accounts to include ecosystem accounting (United Nations et al., 2021a). This accounting framework facilitates the establishment of environmental goals, policy design, progress monitoring and evaluation, covering sustainability issues from biodiversity to climate change, and is recognized in international commitments such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the SDGs (L. Hein, Bagstad, et al., 2020). Natural capital accounting addresses sustainable development and sustainable use of natural resources in general by enabling the accounting of the non-market benefits of nature, but it is not specifically linked to one particular nexus element. Rather, a broad variety of topics that involve nexus elements and interactions can be addressed using the natural capital accounting concept, such as land use planning, green economic growth or designing policy measures (taxes, regulations) (L. Hein, Bagstad, et al., 2020; Ruijs et al., 2019). In developing nations, the focus is mainly on energy and water accounts due to data challenges, while developed countries prioritize accounts on material flows, environmental taxes and subsidies, especially concerning energy. This contrast reflects differing environmental priorities, implementation rates and the focus of account compilation, as well as disparities in funding and access to technical assistance (Pirmana et al., 2019). The effectiveness of natural capital accounting in shaping real-world economic policies requires further refinement and closer integration with economic models (Bagstad et al., 2021; Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, 2020). Additionally, criticisms of the System of Environmental Economic Accounting framework for its top-down approach and exclusion of embracing traditional and biocentric knowledge underscores the need for methodological enhancements. Adopting an integrated valuation of ecosystem services as a methodological enhancement could more accurately reflect previously excluded knowledge and overlooked sociocultural values and IPLC perspectives (Gómez-Baggethun et al., 2014; Pascual et al., 2017).

title: Finance for water infrastructure
definition: This response options cluster includes (i) improving water accounting; (ii) mobilizing financial resources for investment in infrastructure, human capital and institutional capacities for integrated water management (including mobilization of private sector expertise in these areas); (iii) stimulating innovative financing systems with environmental and social safeguards and regulation, (iv) establishing enabling conditions for financial viability and creditworthiness of water sector, and (v) advancing climate actions through mitigation and adaptation actions in the water sector (Boelee et al., 2017; OECD, 2022; The World Bank, 2023). Financing water infrastructure for integrated water management occurs from local to national scales, with examples from Europe (Berbel & Expósito, 2020; Borrego-Marín et al., 2016; Edens & Graveland, 2014; United Nations, 2012), North America (Lazurko & Venema, 2017) and the Global South (Garrick et al., 2020). However, evidence on their benefit to biodiversity is unresolved (e.g., reduction in freshwater biodiversity and ecosystem services; Russi et al., 2013). Market-based water quality trading programs are also a mechanism for using price signals in river-basin management (Abdalla et al., 2007; Corrales et al., 2013; Tabaichount et al., 2019). Water quality and pollution trading in some markets might create incentives for more sustainable food production as farmers reduce water pollution (Zapata et al., 2023), but this has not been the case in much of the United States of America (Gasper et al., 2012). A review of water quality trading practices found that the implementation of these programs is complex with institutional, regulatory, environmental, economic and social factors contributing to the success or failure of these programs (H. Liu & Brouwer, 2023). Water banking, or use of an intermediary acting between buyers and sellers of water rights to facilitate market transfers, is another promising response to drought and other water crises (Barbier, 2022; Montilla-López et al., 2016). The benefits of water-related economic instruments for achieving nexus-wide benefits are generally unresolved. However, economic instruments have been shown to help in increasing irrigation water efficiency by reducing water demand. For example, increases in irrigation water price led farms to choose rainfed crops in northern Spain (Aldaya et al., 2023), and a 1-10 per cent increase in water pricing in Europe and the United States of America reduced water consumption by 10-48 per cent (Reynaud, 2015; Scheierling et al., 2006). Economic incentives also have been used to determine crop rotations that reduce water consumption (Hulugalle & Scott, 2008). Blended finance can also play a critical role in mobilizing commercial finance to achieve SDG6 (water and sanitation for all) (OECD, 2019) and hence have co-benefits for health (SDG3). At the same time, implementation of economic instruments is challenging due to the common pool nature of water use and their lack of fit with abatement pollution measures (i.e., for non-point source pollution where water pricing may not be tied to the polluter) and overall effectiveness in ensuring efficiency and equity (Albiac et al., 2020; de Andrade Resende Filho et al., 2015; Pigram, 1999). Recognizing multiple values of water (Grafton et al., 2023), including non-market water values, in water accounts and financing are key components of transformative pathways towards more sustainable water futures. For example, the impacts of water resource development on Australian Indigenous customary economies have been assessed using replacement cost methods (Jackson et al., 2014). Economics, pricing and financing can be transformational in global water allocation in terms of by whom, what, where and when water is used (Grafton et al., 2020, 2023; United Nations, 2021).

title: Reform public spending
definition: When agricultural products or processes have externalities, two public instruments for including those characteristics in the market price are subsidies (for positive externalities, e.g., soil erosion reduction) and taxes (for negative externalities, e.g., practices generating health or environmental problems). Nevertheless, many countries implement agricultural subsidies, mainly focused on commodity crops and fisheries, which are mostly harmful to human health and the environment as they promote unsustainable practices (FAO, UNDP, et al., 2021). Most harmful subsidies influence international market costs and supply, distorting free trade rules and impacting small farmers in developing countries (DeBoe et al., 2020; FAO, UNDP, et al., 2021; Shetty & Winch, 2015; Swain, 2009; Vos et al., 2022). Three of them are particularly important: (1) subsidies coupled with production inputs and/or outputs that promote commodity production even when market prices are below production costs; (2) market price support acting as border measures (e.g., tariffs, licenses and quotas) that increase or decrease domestic prices; and (3) subsidies decoupled from production inputs or outputs that may or may not be associated with agri-environmental practices (Ash & Cox, 2022; DeBoe, 2020; DeBoe et al., 2020; FAO, UNDP, et al., 2021; Vos et al., 2022). Agricultural subsidies are estimated to be $540 billion per year and rise to $1.8 trillion per year by 2030 under a business-as-usual scenario (FAO, UNDP, et al., 2021). Implicit subsidies (in the form of hidden costs or negative externalities) of food systems are estimated to be at least $12.4 trillion per year (with a range of $5.3 trillion to $19.8 trillion) valued at 12.4 per cent of global gross domestic product (Damania et al., 2023; FAO, UNDP, et al., 2021; FOLU, 2019; Hendriks et al., 2021). title: Global cooperation for finance and technology
definition: Global cooperation in finance and technology is pivotal for climate action, with international partnerships and commitments acting as central catalysts (G. Bianco et al., 2022). Public and private financing shapes adaptive strategies and mitigation efforts, crucial in climate-vulnerable sectors. The commitment by the Conference of the Parties the UNFCCC at its 15th meeting (COP 15) to mobilize $100 billion annually by 2020 for climate action in developing countries highlights this effort, despite a continuing shortfall acknowledged at 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference, where contributions reached only $89.6 billion by 2021, and favoured mitigation over adaptation (OECD, 2022; UNFCCC, 2021). The UNEP adaptation gap report underscores the inadequacy of current financing, estimating necessary adaptation costs at $194 to $366 billion annually, far surpassing current flows of finance (United Nations Environment Programme, 2023). Efforts to balance financial allocations between adaptation and mitigation according to the Paris Agreement have seen calls for developed nations to double their adaptation finance by 2025 from 2019 levels (UNFCCC, 2021). The glaring financial gap hinders effective adaptation in developing countries, necessitating increased contributions from both developed and developing nations, with the latter focusing on earmarked allocations for climate interventions (Carty et al., 2020; Singh & Chudasama, 2021b). The looming economic impact of climate-related loss and damage, projected between $290 and $580 billion by 2030, emphasizes the urgency of operationalizing finance facilities for loss and damage (Markandya & González-Eguino, 2019). The interconnectedness of climate and biodiversity finance is apparent, with target 19 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework advocating for a significant increase in biodiversity funding (currently around $200 billion annually), aiming to bridge the funding gap of at least $0.3 to 1 trillion and aligning financial strategies for climate and biodiversity to achieve broader sustainability goals (CBD, 2023; Dempsey et al., 2022; Deutz et al., 2020). Moreover, there is an urgent need to mainstream technology transfer into finance, particularly to operationalize the technology transfer provisions established by the UNFCCC, such as the Climate Technology Centre and Network. This could involve exemptions from patentability or compulsory licensing to facilitate benefit-sharing (Sharman, 2022). Countries with poor intellectual property rights (IPR) protections have fewer initiatives (Weko & Goldthau, 2022) as low-carbon technology patents are mostly held by the Global North which is an impediment for the Global South to decarbonize (C. Zhou, 2019). At the 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference the fiscal constraints and increasing costs to adapt were acknowledged, and the need for public and grant-based resources for adaptation in developing country Parties was reiterated (UNFCCC, 2024). Technological cooperation is essential for ensuring equitable access to resources and adaptive strategies, fostering innovation and mitigating the effects of climate change. Addressing intellectual property rights and promoting open innovation are necessary to lower deployment costs of low-carbon technologies, integrating them as global public goods (G. Bianco et al., 2022). Strengthening international collaboration in technology transfer enables developing countries to meet their climate commitments while contributing to sustainable development goals, though challenges remain in ensuring equitable benefits from global technology development (Lema et al., 2021; Nightingale et al., 2020; Ockwell & Byrne, 2016).

title: Multilateral environmental agreements
definition: Multilateral environmental agreements provide powerful solutions to transboundary problems through collective action that can involve all elements of the nexus. As national priorities are often divided, such global guidance solutions are a key tool for providing regulatory framings and focus on conservation priorities, as seen in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (I. J. Visseren-Hamakers & Kok, 2022). However, effective implementation is often lacking (Independent Group of Scientists appointed by the Secretary-General, 2019). Over 747 MEAs have been produced within the last 150 years creating a complex network of agreements that makes implementation challenging (Kim, 2013), amplified by the sectoral approach taken (Chasek & Wagner, 2012; Kim & Bosselmann, 2013). For example, a recent review of 195 Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement reported that none of the commitments mention of synergies or trade-offs with biodiversity or land degradation goals (Schmidt-Traub et al., 2021). While multilateral environmental agreements should be formulated using clear transboundary goals (Kim & Bosselmann, 2013), their implementation at the national level gains resilience (i.e., implementation is more likely to succeed and be long-lasting) when undertaken with flexibility and responsiveness to local needs and knowledge (Akhtar-Schuster et al., 2011; Steiner et al., 2003). title: Reconnecting people with nature
definition: Reconnecting people with nature encompasses the idea of restoring or fostering a deep connection between humans and natural environments. In current societies, many people have become increasingly disconnected from nature due to urbanization, technology and lifestyles (Soga & Gaston, 2016). This disconnection has negative impacts on mental and physical health, particularly among people in Western societies and cities, and on environmental awareness and conservation efforts (Barragan-Jason et al., 2023). Efforts to reconnect people with nature include outdoor education programs, physical activity in nature, green space management or gardening in urban areas, nature-based spiritual practices or therapies, sustainable living practices, nature-based arts and crafts, and environmental advocacy (Coventry et al., 2021; Ives et al., 2018). These efforts can be supported by government agencies developing green spaces in cities, environmental NGOs facilitating nature-based experience, healthcare providers promoting nature-based therapies, or educational institutions integrating outdoor learning into curricula (Barragan-Jason et al., 2022). Most activities to reconnect people with nature contribute to diverse types of connections and have multiple effects on the nexus elements. For example, community gardens reconnect people with nature through material (e.g., food) and experiential connections (sensory) and contribute to cognitive (knowledge, inspiration) or emotional connections (feelings, appreciation) (Rigolon et al., 2021). Among the various types of knowledge that can be mobilized when reconnecting with nature, ILK is crucial because it offers cultural perspectives and practices that can foster a deeper understanding and appreciation of the natural world (Burgos-Ayala et al., 2020). As evidenced from 1990 case studies synthesized in 23 reviews and meta-analyses, reconnecting people with nature yields numerous benefits for the nexus elements: direct benefits on health, food and biodiversity, as well as indirect benefits for water and climate change. However, scientific evidence is often geographically and socially biased towards Western societies and urban populations. While physical and mental health, cognitive performance and pro-environmental behaviours garner substantial attention, social and spiritual benefits remain underexplored, despite their significant potential implications (Keniger et al., 2013). Reconnecting people with nature has well-established positive impacts on physical and mental health (Barragan-Jason et al., 2022). Physical connections improve health by boosting activity levels and providing additional benefits such as lowered blood pressure, cortisol reduction, enhanced immune function and faster recovery from illness or surgery (Twohig-Bennett & Jones, 2018). Mental health benefits derive from both improved physical health (Ohrnberger et al., 2017) and direct exposure to nature. For example, activities such as walking or running in natural settings can alleviate anxiety, anger or sadness (Bowler et al., 2010), while natural sounds such as water or bird songs can reduce stress and enhance positive moods (Buxton et al., 2021). Effective nature-based interventions such as gardening, green exercise and nature therapy further improve mood and reduce anxiety (Coventry et al., 2021). However, connections with nature can also have negative physical impacts (e.g., animal attacks) (Soga & Gaston, 2022), as well as psychological impacts (e.g., eco-anxiety, Coffey et al., 2021). The need to reconnect people with nature incentivizes nature protection and habitat restoration, with positive impacts on biodiversity, water and climate change. For example, urban green spaces designed for enhancing well-being can also benefit urban biodiversity, water regulation, carbon sequestration and climate change adaptation (Barragan-Jason et al., 2022). However, these benefits can have adverse effects, including the overuse of water or pesticides in community gardens (Raneng et al., 2023), the carbon footprint of travelling to natural areas and degradation due to overcrowding in protected areas (Birendra, 2022). Reconnecting people with nature can also directly benefit food production and access to healthy food. Community gardens enhance access to fresh produce and promote values of food sharing and cooking (M. T. Garcia et al., 2018). Nature-based therapies may involve preparing food from natural products (Rigolon et al., 2021), whereas hikes in natural areas offer opportunities for foraging wild foods (Schulp et al., 2014). Reconnecting people with nature influences attitudes and behaviours, leading to pro-environmental actions that indirectly benefit biodiversity, water resources and climate change (L. B. Miller et al., 2022). Individuals feeling connected to nature are more inclined to use climate-friendly transportation, renewable energies and eco-friendly products, to care for animals, to support local biodiversity protection initiatives, or to volunteer for conservation (Mackay & Schmitt, 2019). Furthermore, the physical and mental health benefits derived from connecting with nature can enhance people's capacity to adapt to climate change (Wamsler & Brink, 2018). Reconnecting people with nature is considered economically efficient, as it leads to health improvements that can reduce the high economic and social costs associated with physical and mental health problems (Coventry et al., 2021; Kotera et al., 2022). Strengthening physical and psychological connections with nature can be accomplished at a moderate cost through targeted interventions, such as developing urban greenspaces, greening schoolyards or facilitating access to nature (e.g., transportation, information, education) and to nature-based mindfulness activities (Barragan-Jason et al., 2022). It can also reduce environmental injustice by improving equitable access to green spaces and natural areas for all communities (Rigolon et al., 2021). Such initiatives must address the widespread inequities in physical access to nature, especially in cities, which stem from spatially-skewed distribution of green spaces among socioeconomic groups, transportation costs and lack of resources (Y. Sun et al., 2022). Additionally, environmental education to promote psychological connections to nature can reduce existing inequities in childhood experiences or education about nature.

title: Nature on prescription
definition: Health promotion through contact with nature is supported by nature on prescription and nature-based health interventions when healthcare professionals refer individual patients or groups with a range of health conditions to activities in nature (Adewuyi et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023). There is increasing evidence that the natural environment promotes health through supporting physical activity, reducing stress and/or depression, prevention or treatment of obesity and diabetes, cooling during heat waves, and improved quality of life, well-being and social support (Marselle et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021). This includes blue (water) and green spaces as healing environments. Natural environments also enable beneficial contact with microbial biodiversity and associated health benefits. Research on health benefits of nature contact is not distributed evenly geographically. Mental health benefits are mainly reported in Europe and Asia, suggesting a bias (Beute et al., 2023). Risk of tick-borne diseases in some regions also highlights the existence of negative consequences (Heylen et al., 2019). Nature-based health interventions can support biodiversity conservation when combined with increased nature connectedness and pro-environmental behaviour (E. A. Martin et al., 2019; White et al., 2020) but can also put pressure on biodiversity. This became more apparent in the lockdowns during the COVID pandemic (Ferguson et al., 2023). Nature on prescription can promote use of greenspace during heat waves, e.g., among vulnerable groups like the elderly (Arnberger et al., 2017; Kabisch et al., 2021). Health benefits of community gardening (Howarth et al., 2020; Koay & Dillon, 2020; Malberg Dyg et al., 2020) and care (or social) farms (Hassink et al., 2014; Moruzzo et al., 2019) are relevant to nature on prescription. Nature on prescription is emerging as a complementary healthcare approach (Adewuyi et al., 2023; Buckley et al., 2020; Kondo, Oyekanmi, et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2023; Robinson & Breed, 2019), and can be applied globally. For example, nature on prescription is gaining interest from the healthcare sector (e.g., in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (NHS, 2023) and Canada (PaRx, 2023)) but is far from common practice (Astell-Burt et al., 2023) and needs implementation and evaluation research (Buckley et al., 2020). Access inequalities through gentrification (Anguelovski et al., 2022) and unequal accessibility to natural areas (Rigolon et al., 2018) can impact equity of nature on prescription. In terms of avoided healthcare costs, it has the potential to contribute significantly at a population level to address non-communicable diseases (A. C. Santos et al., 2023), as well as in decreasing the environmental footprint of the healthcare sector (Andrieu et al., 2023; Lenzen et al., 2020; Pichler et al., 2019; Seppänen & Or, 2023). However, nature on prescription cost-effective studies are currently lacking (Hinde et al., 2021). Nature on prescription is potentially consistent with ILK, inclusive and participatory. There is limited evidence of transformative change potential for this response option alone, though when combined with other initiatives for example through nature connectedness, nature conservation, community garden activities and social prescription (Bickerdike et al., 2017) it has significant transformative potential.

title: Integrated health education
definition: Planetary Health, One Health, EcoHealth and related approaches seek to transform how health is conceptualized within Earth system functions, across species and cultural world views. Curricula for teaching these approaches exist and, while not identical, are complementary and potentially converging (Buse et al., 2018). Currently, Planetary Health, which situates human health within Earth system function (Horton et al., 2014), and One Health, which aims to achieve optimal health for humans, animals and ecosystems (OHLEPP et al., 2022), are most commonly taught. Even more traditional fields of Global Health reference these approaches so there may be future convergence of these curricula (Laing et al., 2023). The curricula primarily address human health priorities within the nexus (for water, food, climate change mitigation and adaptation) and for biodiversity the focus is on risks and protective pathways. Key features of Planetary Health and One Health published curricula are shown in Box. Approaches to education that frame health across scale, species and cultures are potentially highly transformative by building capacity for new ways of thinking and addressing problems. Technical feasibility is high as these curricula are already being taught in multiple countries. Costs are equivalent in comparison to similar professional education. Education for sustainability and climate change issues specifically addresses SDG target 4.7. Distributional, inclusion and procedural equity should continue to be carefully reviewed for these curricula as their early development was predominantly in the Global North (where societies are least sustainable). Pre-tertiary integrated health education could be highly beneficial in changing world views and responsibility more broadly. NEXUS GOVERNANCE TO SUPPORT HEALTH RESPONSE OPTIONS Health system governance refers to the rules and norms that shape roles and responsibilities, incentives and interactions in the health sector. A variety of conventions, cultural traditions, economic and environmental pressures influence governance arrangements and health system performance. These include new partnerships that recognize traditional health practices and new conceptual models of health such as Planetary Health and One Health. Good health and well-being are core values for society alongside sociocultural, economic and biophysical values (Pascual et al., 2017). They cannot be achieved in isolation and hence nexus governance is required. Response option implementation The 15 response options considered in this subchapter are directly implementable on the ground and embody action or management that can advance health while providing co-benefits for other nexus elements.6 Evidence documented in this subchapter shows that while response options are themselves enabled by various types of policy instruments, these also serve to advance and guide action to achieve multiple policy objectives beyond health. The choice of the most appropriate policy instrument will be context dependent. This is particularly the case for response options H04 to H11 and H14 where different types or combinations of policy instruments may be needed to action or enable the option on the ground depending on context.
